RESPIRATORY__Foundations of Respiratory:
Overview — Mechanics of Ventilation
Ventilation = moving air in and out of the lungs — a mechanical process driven by pressure gradients created by changing the volume of the thorax.
The organising principle: air flows down pressure gradients (Boyle's law — ↑volume → ↓pressure → air flows in). Breathing changes thoracic volume; the lung's elastic recoil + the chest wall's outward pull set up the forces to overcome.
Why it matters: underpins obstructive vs restrictive disease, pneumothorax, work of breathing, and COPD/asthma/fibrosis behaviour — cross-ref lung volumes/spirometry, COPD, asthma, pneumothorax, respiratory failure.
The Pressures Involved — breathing is pressure differences
Pressure What it is Key point
AtmosphericOutside air (reference, = 0)Air flows in when alveolar P < this
Alveolar (intrapulmonary)Inside the alveoliNegative in inspiration (draws air in), positive in expiration
IntrapleuralIn the pleural spaceAlways negative (~−5 cmH₂O) — the "vacuum" holding the lung open against the chest wall
TranspulmonaryAlveolar − intrapleuralThe distending pressure keeping alveoli open
The intrapleural negative pressure is the key concept: the lung tends to collapse inward (elastic recoil), the chest wall tends to spring outward — these opposing pulls create a negative intrapleural pressure that keeps the lung expanded.
This is why a pneumothorax collapses the lung: air entering the pleural space abolishes the negative pressure → the lung recoils shut.
The Mechanics of a Breath
Inspiration (active)
  • Diaphragm contracts + descends (the main muscle, ~⅔ of the work) + external intercostals lift the ribs ("bucket handle")
  • → thoracic volume ↑ → intrapleural pressure more negative → alveolar pressure falls below atmospheric → air flows in
  • Accessory muscles (sternocleidomastoid, scalenes) recruited in exertion/distress — the clinical sign of ↑work of breathing
Expiration (passive at rest)
  • Muscles relax → elastic recoil pulls the lung back → thoracic volume ↓ → alveolar pressure rises above atmospheric → air flows out
  • Forced expiration is active: internal intercostals + abdominal muscles (exercise, COPD)
Compliance — how stretchy the lung is
Compliance = change in volume per unit change in pressure (how easily the lung expands). It changes oppositely in the two big disease categories:
Compliance Disease Mechanism
↑ compliance (too stretchy, poor recoil)Emphysema (COPD)Destroyed elastic tissue → lungs over-distend, air trapping
↓ compliance (stiff, hard to inflate)Pulmonary fibrosis, oedema, ARDSStiff/fibrotic or fluid-filled lung
Surfactant's role: produced by type II pneumocytes, it reduces alveolar surface tension → prevents collapse + increases compliance → less work to inflate. Surfactant deficiency in prematurity → neonatal respiratory distress syndrome (stiff lungs, alveolar collapse).
Surface Tension & Laplace's Law — why surfactant matters
  • Alveoli are fluid-lined → surface tension tends to collapse them
  • Laplace's law: pressure to keep a bubble open ∝ tension / radius → small alveoli have higher collapsing pressure → would empty into large ones
  • Surfactant solves this: it lowers surface tension more in small alveoli → stabilises them, prevents collapse, and equalises pressures across different-sized alveoli
Resistance & the Work of Breathing — the obstructive side
  • Airway resistance governs flow (like the vascular Poiseuille r⁴ point — radius dominates): bronchoconstriction, mucus, or airway narrowing ↑ resistance → ↑work of breathing
  • The obstructive disease link: asthma (bronchospasm), COPD (airway narrowing + collapse) → ↑airway resistance → expiratory flow limitation (air trapping; expiration is the problem → prolonged expiratory phase + wheeze)
  • Work of breathing = overcoming (a) elastic forces (compliance — high in fibrosis) + (b) resistive forces (airway resistance — high in asthma/COPD); raised in both disease types but for different reasons

Overview — Lung Volumes & Spirometry
Lung volumes quantify how much air the lungs hold and move; spirometry measures them to characterise lung disease.
The organising principle: the mechanics from the previous note (compliance, airway resistance) translate into measurable volumes and flow rates — and the single most useful output is the FEV1/FVC ratio, which separates obstructive from restrictive disease.
Why it matters: how COPD, asthma and fibrosis are diagnosed and monitored — cross-ref mechanics of ventilation, COPD, asthma, pulmonary fibrosis, restrictive disease.
Lung Volumes & Capacities
Volumes are single; capacities are sums of volumes.

The "can't measure" point: RV, FRC, and TLC include residual volume → spirometry can't measure them (you can't blow out the air that stays behind) → they need body plethysmography or helium dilution.

Reversibility — Asthma vs COPD
Bronchodilator reversibility testing: give salbutamol and repeat spirometry.
Asthma
Reversible obstruction → FEV1 improves significantly (≥12% + 200 mL) → variable/reversible airflow limitation.
COPD
Largely irreversible → little improvement → fixed airflow limitation.
A core part of distinguishing the two obstructive diseases (cross-ref asthma/COPD).
Flow-Volume Loops & PEFR
  • Flow-volume loop (flow vs volume during a forced breath) — the shape is diagnostic:
    • Obstructive: scooped-out/concave expiratory limb (COPD/asthma)
    • Restrictive: tall narrow loop (small volumes, preserved flows)
    • Upper airway obstruction: flattened loop
  • Peak Expiratory Flow Rate (PEFR): the fastest expiratory flow — a simple bedside/home measure; used to monitor asthma (diurnal variability, treatment response)
Other Useful Measures
  • Transfer factor (TLCO/DLCO) — gas transfer capacity (CO uptake): ↓ in emphysema + fibrosis (loss of functioning alveolar-capillary surface), ↑ in alveolar haemorrhage (extra haemoglobin to bind CO) — ties to the gas exchange note
  • FRC is the physiologically important "resting" volume — where inward lung recoil balances outward chest-wall pull (from the mechanics note)

Overview — Gas Exchange & Diffusion
Gas exchange = transfer of O₂ from alveoli into blood and CO₂ from blood into alveoli, across the alveolar-capillary membrane.
The organising principle: gases move by passive diffusion down partial-pressure gradients — driven by the partial-pressure difference and governed by the membrane's properties (Fick's law).
Why it matters: explains the two types of respiratory failure, why fibrosis/oedema/emphysema cause hypoxia, and the basis of the transfer factor — cross-ref mechanics + spirometry, V/Q matching, respiratory failure, pneumonia, fibrosis, the O₂-dissociation curve.
The Alveolar-Capillary Membrane
  • Gas exchange occurs across the extremely thin respiratory membrane: alveolar epithelium (type I pneumocytes) + fused basement membranes + capillary endothelium — only ~0.5 µm thick
  • Designed for diffusion: huge surface area (~70 m²), very thin, richly perfused — optimised for rapid gas transfer
  • The membrane is what fails in disease: thickening (fibrosis, oedema) or loss of surface area (emphysema, pneumonia) impairs diffusion
Fick's Law of Diffusion — the governing equation
Rate of diffusion ∝ (surface area × partial-pressure gradient × solubility) / membrane thickness.
Factor ↑Diffusion Impaired in
Surface areaLarger = more transferEmphysema (alveolar destruction), pneumonectomy
Membrane thicknessThinner = fasterFibrosis, pulmonary oedema (thickened/fluid-filled)
Partial-pressure gradientBigger = more transferAltitude (↓inspired O₂), hypoventilation
Gas solubilityMore soluble = faster(explains the CO₂ vs O₂ difference below)
Clinical payoff: every diffusion-impairing disease works through one of these — fibrosis/oedema = ↑thickness, emphysema = ↓surface area → both reduce the transfer factor (TLCO).
CO₂ vs O₂ — the key asymmetry
  • CO₂ is ~20× more soluble than O₂ → it diffuses far more readily
  • The consequence: in diffusion-limited disease (fibrosis), O₂ transfer fails before CO₂ transfer → hypoxia occurs early, CO₂ retention is late → early lung disease causes hypoxia with a normal or low CO₂
  • CO₂ removal is ventilation-dependent (it diffuses easily, so its clearance depends on how much you breathe), whereas O₂ uptake is more diffusion-dependent — this underlies the two types of respiratory failure
Partial Pressures & the Gradients
Alveolus Venous (arriving) Arterial (leaving)
O₂~13.3 kPa (100 mmHg)~5.3 kPa~13 kPa (equilibrated)
CO₂~5.3 kPa (40 mmHg)~6.1 kPa~5.3 kPa (equilibrated)
  • O₂ diffuses alveolus → blood (down its gradient); CO₂ diffuses blood → alveolus (down its gradient)
  • Equilibration is normally complete well before blood leaves the capillary (lots of reserve) — so diffusion problems only show under stress (exercise) until severe
  • The alveolar gas equation (concept): alveolar O₂ depends on inspired O₂ minus the CO₂ being added — the basis for the A–a gradient
The A–a Gradient & Types of Respiratory Failure
The alveolar-arterial (A–a) gradient = difference between alveolar O₂ and arterial O₂; it tells you whether the problem is in the lung (gas exchange) or in ventilation.

MechanismGas exchange failure (V/Q mismatch, diffusion defect, shunt)Ventilatory failure (not moving enough air)

The CO₂ logic: in Type 1 the highly-soluble CO₂ still clears (often blown off → low CO₂), only O₂ fails; in Type 2, ventilation itself fails → CO₂ accumulates. Raised A–a gradient = the problem is in the lung; normal A–a with hypoxia = hypoventilation (or low inspired O₂).

Overview — Oxygen-Haemoglobin Dissociation Curve
Once O₂ diffuses into the blood, it is carried bound to haemoglobin. The oxygen-haemoglobin dissociation curve describes how saturated Hb is at any given oxygen partial pressure (PaO₂).
The organising principle: the curve is sigmoid (S-shaped), not linear — and that shape is functionally brilliant. It lets Hb load O₂ fully in the lungs (flat top) yet unload it readily in the tissues (steep middle). Shifts in the curve fine-tune O₂ delivery to where it is needed.
Why it matters: explains why SpO₂ can stay normal until PaO₂ falls dangerously, why CO poisoning is lethal, and how acidosis/exercise improve O₂ delivery to tissues — cross-ref gas exchange (previous subtab), CO₂ transport (next), anaemia, CO poisoning.
Oxygen Carriage in Blood — the context
  • O₂ is carried two ways: ~98.5% bound to haemoglobin (1 Hb carries 4 O₂) and ~1.5% dissolved in plasma
  • The implication: O₂ delivery depends overwhelmingly on Hb concentration + Hb saturation, not dissolved O₂ → which is why anaemia reduces O₂ delivery even with a normal PaO₂/SpO₂ (less Hb to carry it)
  • Oxygen content ≈ (Hb × SaO₂ × 1.34) + dissolved — the carriage equation (concept-level)
The Sigmoid Curve & Why the Shape Matters — the core concept
  • Plot: O₂ saturation (SaO₂, %) on the y-axis against PaO₂ on the x-axis → an S-shaped curve
  • The shape is the whole point (cooperative binding — each O₂ that binds makes the next bind more easily):
Part of the curve PaO₂ range Functional significance
Flat upper portion (plateau)high PaO₂ (lungs, ~8–13 kPa)Loading: Hb stays ~fully saturated even if PaO₂ drops somewhat → a safety margin (you can lose a lot of PaO₂ before SaO₂ falls)
Steep middle portionlower PaO₂ (tissues, ~2.5–5.5 kPa)Unloading: a small drop in tissue PaO₂ releases a lot of O₂ → efficient delivery where metabolism is high
The clinical "flat top" payoff (high-yield): because the top is flat, SpO₂ can stay >90% until PaO₂ has already fallen substantially → by the time saturation drops, oxygenation is already significantly impaired (a falling SpO₂ is a late warning). Conversely, giving extra O₂ to an already-saturated patient adds little (you are on the plateau).
Shifts of the Curve — the fine-tuning (high-yield)
The curve shifts left (Hb holds O₂ more tightly — higher affinity) or right (Hb releases O₂ more readily — lower affinity):
RIGHT shift (↓affinity → unloads O₂ to tissues) LEFT shift (↑affinity → holds O₂)
↑CO₂↓CO₂

The Bohr effect (the key one): actively metabolising tissue produces CO₂, acid, and heat → shifts the curve right → Hb unloads more O₂ exactly where it is needed most (working muscle) — an elegant feedback. The lungs do the reverse (blow off CO₂ → left shift → loading).
Mnemonic: "right = release" (a right shift releases O₂); a right shift is generally good for tissue delivery.
The High-Yield Special Cases — left shifts that matter clinically
Fetal haemoglobin (HbF)
  • Left-shifted (higher O₂ affinity than adult HbA) → lets the fetus pull O₂ from maternal blood across the placenta (fetal Hb grabs O₂ that maternal Hb releases)
Carbon monoxide (the lethal one)
  • CO binds Hb with ~250× the affinity of O₂ → forms carboxyhaemoglobin, and left-shifts the curve (the remaining O₂ is held more tightly, released less) → a double hit: less O₂ carried and less released to tissues
  • The CO/SpO₂ trap: pulse oximetry cannot distinguish COHb from O₂Hb → SpO₂ reads falsely normal in CO poisoning → need co-oximetry (cross-ref CO poisoning/toxicology)

Overview — CO₂ Transport
CO₂ produced by tissue metabolism must be carried in the blood to the lungs for excretion — and it is transported three ways, dominated by conversion to bicarbonate.
The organising principle: most CO₂ travels as bicarbonate (HCO₃⁻), generated inside red cells by carbonic anhydrase — which is why CO₂ transport and acid-base balance are the same chemistry (CO₂ + water ⇌ carbonic acid ⇌ bicarbonate + H⁺).
Why it matters: the bridge between respiratory physiology and acid-base balance — it explains respiratory acidosis/alkalosis, the bicarbonate buffer, and CO₂ retention in respiratory failure — cross-ref O₂ dissociation curve (previous subtab), acid-base balance, respiratory failure, COPD.
The Three Forms of CO₂ Transport — the spine
Form Proportion Mechanism
Bicarbonate (HCO₃⁻)~70% (the majority)CO₂ + H₂O → carbonic acid → HCO₃⁻ + H⁺ (in red cells, via carbonic anhydrase)
Carbamino compounds (bound to Hb)~23%CO₂ binds the globin part of haemoglobin (not the haem — so does not compete with O₂)
Dissolved~7%Dissolved in plasma (more than O₂, as CO₂ is more soluble)
The key point: unlike O₂ (which is mostly Hb-bound), CO₂ is mostly carried as bicarbonate — and that conversion is the link to acid-base.
The Bicarbonate Mechanism — the core chemistry (high-yield)
In the tissues (where CO₂ is high), inside the red blood cell:
CO₂ + H₂O ⇌ H₂CO₃ ⇌ HCO₃⁻ + H⁺
(the central equation — memorise this)
  • Driven by carbonic anhydrase (the enzyme that makes this fast — concentrated in red cells)
  • CO₂ diffuses into the red cell → carbonic anhydrase converts it to carbonic acid → dissociates into HCO₃⁻ + H⁺
  • HCO₃⁻ exits the cell into plasma (the main transport form), in exchange for Cl⁻ entering — the "chloride shift" (maintains electrical neutrality)
  • The H⁺ is buffered by haemoglobin inside the cell (Hb is a good buffer)
In the lungs, it all reverses: low CO₂ → HCO₃⁻ + H⁺ recombine → CO₂ → diffuses out into the alveoli → exhaled.
The Haldane Effect — the CO₂ counterpart to the Bohr effect
Deoxygenated haemoglobin carries CO₂ better than oxygenated Hb (deoxy-Hb is a better buffer for H⁺ and binds more carbamino-CO₂).
The functional elegance (pairs with the Bohr effect)
  • In tissues: Hb releases O₂ (becomes deoxygenated) → now carries CO₂ more readily → picks up CO₂ where it is produced
  • In lungs: Hb binds O₂ (becomes oxygenated) → releases CO₂ → dumps CO₂ where it is exhaled
The two effects work together: Bohr = CO₂/acid promotes O₂ unloading (tissues); Haldane = O₂ promotes CO₂ unloading (lungs) — a reciprocal system optimising both gases at both ends.
The Link to Acid-Base — the most important conceptual payoff
The central equation CO₂ + H₂O ⇌ HCO₃⁻ + H⁺ means CO₂ directly determines blood [H⁺] / pH:
Change Equation shift Result
↑CO₂ (hypoventilation/retention)shifts right↑H⁺ → ↓pH → respiratory acidosis
↓CO₂ (hyperventilation)shifts left↓H⁺ → ↑pH → respiratory alkalosis
This is why the lungs are a rapid pH regulator: changing ventilation changes CO₂ → changes pH within minutes (the respiratory compensation for metabolic disturbances) — cross-ref acid-base.
The Henderson-Hasselbalch concept: pH depends on the ratio of HCO₃⁻ (metabolic/renal) to CO₂ (respiratory) — the lungs control the CO₂, the kidneys control the HCO₃⁻.
CO₂ and the Control of Breathing — why CO₂ drives ventilation
  • CO₂ is the main stimulus to breathe (via central chemoreceptors sensing CSF pH, which tracks CO₂) — rising CO₂ → ↑ventilation → blows off CO₂
  • The COPD caveat (high-yield): in chronic CO₂ retainers, the chemoreceptors become desensitised to CO₂ and the drive shifts partly to hypoxia ("hypoxic drive") → why high-flow O₂ can reduce respiratory drive in some CO₂-retaining COPD patients (target SpO₂ 88–92%)

Overview — Control of Breathing
Breathing is automatic (you do not think about it) yet adjustable (you can override it, and it adapts to demand) — controlled by a brainstem rhythm generator modulated by chemical and mechanical feedback.
The organising principle: the system works by negative feedback — chemoreceptors sense blood gases/pH, the brainstem sets the rhythm, and ventilation adjusts to keep CO₂ (and pH) constant. The dominant signal is CO₂, not O₂.
Why it matters: explains the CO₂/hypoxic drive, why opioids cause respiratory depression, Cheyne-Stokes/Kussmaul breathing, and the COPD oxygen-target controversy — cross-ref CO₂ transport (previous subtab), acid-base, respiratory failure, COPD, opioid toxicity.

The central chemoreceptor mechanism (high-yield): CO₂ (not H⁺) crosses the blood-brain barrier easily → in the CSF it forms carbonic acid → H⁺ (the CO₂ transport chemistry again) → the ↑CSF [H⁺] stimulates the central chemoreceptors → ↑ventilation → blows off CO₂ → corrects it. The dominance of CO₂: under normal conditions, CO₂ is by far the most powerful stimulus to breathe — tiny rises in PaCO₂ produce large increases in ventilation. O₂ is a backup that only drives breathing when it falls dangerously low.
The Hierarchy of Drive: CO₂ vs O₂ — the high-yield concept

  • O₂ (hypoxic drive, via peripheral chemoreceptors) is the backup — only becomes a significant driver when PaO₂ falls below ~8 kPa
The COPD "hypoxic drive" caveat (the classic exam controversy): in chronic CO₂ retainers (severe COPD), the central chemoreceptors become desensitised to chronically high CO₂ → the patient relies more on the hypoxic drive. Giving high-flow O₂ can theoretically remove that drive → hypoventilation → worsening CO₂ retention → this is why the target SpO₂ is 88–92% in known retainers (controlled oxygen, not none).
(Modern understanding: the mechanism is more complex than pure hypoxic drive — it also involves V/Q changes and the Haldane effect — but the clinical rule [controlled O₂, target 88–92%] stands.)

Overview — Ventilation-Perfusion (V/Q) Matching
Gas exchange needs both air reaching the alveoli (ventilation, V) and blood reaching the capillaries (perfusion, Q) — and the two must be matched for efficient exchange.
The organising principle: the ideal is V/Q ≈ 1 (ventilation matched to perfusion); the two extremes are dead space (ventilation without perfusion, V/Q → ∞) and shunt (perfusion without ventilation, V/Q → 0) — and most lung disease causes hypoxia through V/Q mismatch.
Why it matters: V/Q mismatch is the commonest cause of hypoxaemia, and the dead-space/shunt distinction explains PE vs pneumonia, and why shunt does not correct with oxygen — cross-ref gas exchange (the A–a gradient + 5 causes of hypoxaemia), PE, pneumonia, respiratory failure.
The Two Components — the spine
  • Ventilation (V): the rate air reaches the alveoli (~4 L/min at rest)
  • Perfusion (Q): the rate blood reaches the pulmonary capillaries (~5 L/min = cardiac output)
  • The ratio V/Q ≈ 0.8 overall (close to 1) — the target for efficient gas exchange; matching matters more than the absolute values
The Two Extremes — dead space vs shunt (the conceptual core)
Dead space Shunt
V/Qhigh (→ ∞)low (→ 0)
ProblemVentilation without perfusion — air reaches alveoli but no blood to exchange withPerfusion without ventilation — blood reaches alveoli but no air to exchange with
Analogy"wasted ventilation""wasted perfusion"
Classic causePulmonary embolism (clot blocks perfusion)Consolidation/collapse (alveoli filled/airless but still perfused) — pneumonia, ARDS, atelectasis

The shunt point (high-yield): a true shunt is the one cause of hypoxaemia that does not correct with supplemental oxygen — because the shunted blood never meets ventilated alveoli, so adding O₂ to the alveoli cannot reach it. This distinguishes shunt from V/Q mismatch and diffusion defects (which do respond to O₂).
Types of dead space: anatomical (the conducting airways — trachea/bronchi, ~150 mL, never reach alveoli) + alveolar (ventilated but unperfused alveoli, e.g. PE) = physiological dead space.
Regional V/Q Variation in the Normal Lung — the gravity effect (high-yield)
Even a normal upright lung has a V/Q gradient from apex to base, because gravity affects blood (perfusion) more than air (ventilation):
Region Ventilation Perfusion V/Q Net effect
Apex (top)lowermuch lowerhigh V/Q (~3)relatively over-ventilated (dead-space-like)
Base (bottom)highermuch higherlow V/Q (~0.6)relatively over-perfused (shunt-like)
  • Both V and Q increase down the lung, but perfusion increases more (gravity pulls blood to the base) → so V/Q is high at the apex, low at the base
  • The clinical payoff: this regional variation explains disease distribution — e.g. TB favours the apex (high O₂, high V/Q, relatively poor blood/immune cell delivery)
Hypoxic Pulmonary Vasoconstriction — the lung's auto-correction (high-yield + unique)
The principle: unlike the systemic circulation (where hypoxia causes vasodilation), the pulmonary circulation responds to alveolar hypoxia with vasoconstriction — hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction (HPV).
The purpose: it diverts blood away from poorly-ventilated (low-V/Q) alveoli toward well-ventilated ones → improves V/Q matching → optimises oxygenation.
The clinical consequences
  • It is the lung's mechanism to minimise shunt (redirects perfusion to ventilated areas)
  • Chronic global hypoxia (e.g. COPD, altitude) → widespread HPV → pulmonary hypertension → right heart strain (cor pulmonale)
How V/Q Mismatch Causes Hypoxaemia — the synthesis
  • V/Q mismatch is the commonest cause of hypoxaemia (cross-ref gas exchange note's 5 causes)
  • The lung cannot fully compensate because of the shape of the oxygen-dissociation curve (cross-ref): high-V/Q areas are already on the flat plateau (cannot load extra O₂ to make up for the low-V/Q areas), but low-V/Q areas drop steeply → the net effect is hypoxaemia (the elegant link to the dissociation curve)
  • CO₂ is less affected (more soluble, and ventilation can compensate) → which is why V/Q mismatch tends to cause Type 1 failure (hypoxia with normal/low CO₂)

Overview — Acid-Base Balance (Respiratory & Framework)
The body tightly controls blood pH (normal 7.35–7.45) — even small deviations impair enzyme/protein function, so pH is defended by buffers (instant), the lungs (minutes), and the kidneys (hours-days).
The organising principle: pH is set by the ratio of HCO₃⁻ (metabolic/renal) to CO₂ (respiratory) — the lungs control CO₂, the kidneys control HCO₃⁻. Every acid-base disorder is a problem with one of these, ± compensation by the other.
Why it matters: the framework for interpreting any ABG, and for understanding respiratory failure, DKA, vomiting, COPD, and salicylate poisoning — cross-ref CO₂ transport (the chemistry), control of breathing (compensation), renal acid-base (the renal side), respiratory failure, your clinical acid-base note.
The Central Chemistry — the foundation
CO₂ + H₂O ⇌ H₂CO₃ ⇌ HCO₃⁻ + H⁺ (carbonic anhydrase)
Henderson-Hasselbalch concept: pH ∝ HCO₃⁻ / CO₂ (renal numerator / respiratory denominator)
  • ↑CO₂ → ↑H⁺ → ↓pH (acidosis); ↓CO₂ → ↑pH (alkalosis)
  • ↑HCO₃⁻ → ↑pH (alkalosis); ↓HCO₃⁻ → ↓pH (acidosis)
The Three Lines of Defence — the timescales
Defence Speed Mechanism
BuffersinstantBicarbonate (main extracellular), haemoglobin, proteins, phosphate — soak up H⁺ immediately
Respiratory (lungs)minutesChange ventilation → change CO₂ → change pH (fast compensation)
Renal (kidneys)hours-daysExcrete H⁺ / reabsorb + generate HCO₃⁻ (slow but complete — cross-ref renal acid-base)
The principle: buffers buy time, the lungs respond fast (but only adjust the CO₂/respiratory component), the kidneys respond slowly (but powerfully adjust HCO₃⁻ and are the only route to excrete fixed acid).
The Four Primary Disorders — the core framework
Disorder Primary change pH Cause examples
Respiratory acidosis↑CO₂ (hypoventilation)↓COPD, opioids, neuromuscular, airway obstruction
Respiratory alkalosis↓CO₂ (hyperventilation)↑Anxiety, PE, altitude, early salicylate, pain
Metabolic acidosis↓HCO₃⁻↓DKA, lactic acidosis, renal failure, diarrhoea (cross-ref your anion-gap note)
Metabolic alkalosis↑HCO₃⁻↑Vomiting, diuretics, hyperaldosteronism
The naming logic: "respiratory" = the problem is CO₂ (the lung); "metabolic" = the problem is HCO₃⁻ (everything else); "acidosis/alkalosis" = the direction of pH.
Compensation — how the other system corrects (high-yield)
The principle: if one system causes the problem, the other compensates to pull pH back toward normal — but never fully overcorrects (compensation does not overshoot):
Primary disorder Compensation
Metabolic acidosisRespiratory — hyperventilate to blow off CO₂ (e.g. Kussmaul breathing in DKA) — fast
Metabolic alkalosisRespiratory — hypoventilate to retain CO₂ — limited (cannot stop breathing)
Respiratory acidosisRenal — retain HCO₃⁻ (slow, days — e.g. chronic COPD)
Respiratory alkalosisRenal — excrete HCO₃⁻ (slow)
Acute vs chronic respiratory disorders: the kidney takes days to compensate → so a chronic respiratory acidosis (COPD) has a raised HCO₃⁻ (renal compensation has happened), whereas an acute one does not — the HCO₃⁻ tells you the chronicity (high-yield ABG point).
Respiratory compensation is fast (minutes); renal is slow (days) — which is why metabolic problems get quick respiratory compensation, but respiratory problems take days for renal compensation.
Interpreting an ABG — the practical synthesis (high-yield method)
A stepwise approach
  • 1. pH — acidotic (<7.35) or alkalotic (>7.45)?
  • 2. CO₂ — is it the cause? (↑CO₂ with low pH = respiratory acidosis; ↓CO₂ with high pH = respiratory alkalosis)
  • 3. HCO₃⁻ — is it the cause? (↓HCO₃⁻ with low pH = metabolic acidosis; ↑HCO₃⁻ with high pH = metabolic alkalosis)
  • 4. Compensation — is the other value shifting to correct? (and does pH suggest acute vs chronic / mixed)
  • 5. (Metabolic acidosis) → anion gap — high vs normal (cross-ref your electrolytes/anion-gap note)
The "matching" rule: if CO₂ and HCO₃⁻ move in opposite directions relative to pH → think a mixed disorder; if they move together (one primary, one compensating) → single disorder with compensation.
The Anion Gap — the key metabolic-acidosis subdivision (cross-ref)
Anion gap = (Na⁺) − (Cl⁻ + HCO₃⁻) — separates the causes of metabolic acidosis:
  • Raised anion gap: added acid — lactate, ketones (DKA), urate (renal failure), toxins (methanol, salicylate) — "MUDPILES"
  • Normal anion gap (hyperchloraemic): HCO₃⁻ loss — diarrhoea, RTA, Addison's

Asthma is a chronic inflammatory airway disorder characterised by reversible airflow obstruction and bronchial hyperreactivity. The single most important word is reversibility — this is what distinguishes asthma from COPD (fixed obstruction).

Chronic Asthma
The disease — managed long-term with a stepwise ladder
Acute Asthma
The exacerbation — a severity-stratified emergency
Same disease, two faces. Chronic and acute asthma are inseparable — understanding the chronic disease explains the acute emergency.

Types of Asthma
Allergic / Atopic (most common)
  • IgE-mediated type 1 hypersensitivity
  • The atopic march: eczema → allergic rhinitis / hayfever → asthma
  • Hygiene hypothesis: reduced childhood infections → upregulated Th2 → ↑ allergic disease
Occupational Asthma
  • High molecular weight agents: flour (bakers), latex, grain dust — IgE-mediated
  • Low molecular weight agents: isocyanates (spray painters), colophony, chemicals — non-IgE
  • Diagnostic key: PEF diary — symptoms better on days off / holidays, worse at work
  • Legal implications — must document and notify employer
Aspirin-Induced (Samter's Triad)
  • COX-1 inhibition by aspirin/NSAIDs → ↑ leukotrienes → bronchoconstriction
  • Samter's Triad: asthma + aspirin sensitivity + nasal polyps
  • Classic exam question — know all three components
  • LTRAs (montelukast) particularly useful in this subtype
Exercise-Induced
  • Cold, dry air during exercise → airway cooling → mast cell degranulation
  • Symptoms peak 5–10 minutes after stopping exercise
  • SABA pre-exercise; LTRAs (montelukast) effective add-on
Triggers
  • Viral respiratory infections (commonest trigger in children)
  • Cold air / exercise
  • Allergens: house dust mites, pets, pollen, mould
  • Cigarette smoke / air pollution
  • Night / early morning (diurnal cortisol dip)
  • Strong emotions / stress
  • Beta-blockers (bronchospasm — contraindicated)
  • NSAIDs / aspirin (leukotriene surge)
Beta-blockers are ABSOLUTELY CONTRAINDICATED in asthma — even topical (eye drops for glaucoma). Use with extreme caution in COPD; avoid in asthma.

Classic Symptoms
  • Episodic symptoms with diurnal variation (worse at night / early morning)
  • Dry cough, wheeze, SOB, chest tightness
  • Bilateral polyphonic wheeze on auscultation (expiratory)
  • Atopic history (eczema, hayfever, rhinitis)
  • Symptom-free intervals between episodes

  • Unilateral wheeze — focal lesion / foreign body
  • No response to treatment despite good technique
  • Wheeze only with colds (viral-triggered only — may be viral wheeze, not asthma)
  • Haemoptysis, significant weight loss, clubbing
  • Onset >40 years with smoking history — consider COPD

Overview Banner

COPD is an umbrella term for emphysema + chronic bronchitis + small airway disease. The defining feature is poorly reversible, progressive airflow limitation — the key word is irreversible (vs asthma's reversible).

Chronic COPD
The disease — managed long-term with a stepwise inhaler ladder
Acute Exacerbation (AECOPD)
The emergency — oxygen logic is everything
Cross-ref Asthma: COPD = irreversible, smoker, older, no diurnal variation, BDR <15%. Asthma = reversible, atopic, younger, diurnal variation, BDR >20%. These two are examined as a pair.
Pathophysiology Illustration
Aetiology & Pathophysiology
Causes
  • Smoking — the major cause: inflammation → protease release → parenchymal destruction + inactivates α1-antitrypsin
  • Occupational dust/pollutants (coal, silica, cadmium)
  • Biomass fuels (developing world)
  • Air pollution
  • α1-antitrypsin deficiency — early-onset COPD (<40 yrs), ± FHx, non/minimal smoker; panacinar emphysema affecting lower lobes
Mechanisms
  • Chronic bronchitis: mucus gland hypertrophy, goblet cell hyperplasia, squamous metaplasia → productive cough ≥3 months/yr × 2 yrs
  • Emphysema: protease-mediated destruction of alveolar walls → loss of elastic recoil → air trapping → hyperinflation
  • Small airway disease: inflammation and fibrosis of bronchioles → fixed obstruction
The Two Classic Phenotypes
Pink Puffer (emphysema-predominant)
  • Breathless, not cyanosed, thin, cachexic
  • Pursed-lip breathing, accessory muscles
  • Barrel chest, hyperinflated
  • Maintains near-normal PaO₂ by hyperventilating
Blue Bloater (chronic bronchitis-predominant)
  • Cyanosed, oedematous, overweight
  • CO₂ retainer — bounding pulse, flap (asterixis), warm peripheries, drowsy
  • Cor pulmonale: raised JVP, peripheral oedema
  • Relies on hypoxic drive — O₂ therapy must be controlled

Symptoms
Typical Symptoms
  • Chronic productive cough (smoker's cough) — purulent in infective exacerbation
  • Progressive breathlessness — the dominant symptom, graded by MRC scale
  • Wheeze
  • Weight loss, muscle wasting, depression (extra-pulmonary)
MRC Dyspnoea Scale
  • 1 — Breathless only with strenuous exercise
  • 2 — Short of breath when hurrying on level ground or walking up a hill
  • 3 — Walks slower than contemporaries on level ground due to breathlessness
  • 4 — Stops for breath after walking ~100m on level ground
  • 5 — Too breathless to leave the house / breathless when dressing
Signs of Severe COPD
Respiratory Signs
  • Barrel chest (increased AP diameter from hyperinflation)
  • Loss of cardiac and hepatic dullness to percussion
  • Pursed-lip breathing (creates back-pressure → slows airway collapse)
  • Use of accessory muscles (sternocleidomastoid, scalenes)
  • Prolonged expiratory phase
  • Wheeze and ↓ breath sounds throughout
Signs of CO₂ Retention (Blue Bloater)
  • Bounding pulse (CO₂-mediated vasodilation)
  • Asterixis / flap (CO₂ narcosis)
  • Warm peripheries, plethoric face
  • Drowsiness, confusion
  • Cyanosis (central + peripheral)
  • Cor pulmonale: raised JVP, ankle oedema, RV heave
Spirometry — Diagnostic
Diagnosis requires spirometry: FEV1/FVC <0.7 with no significant reversibility post-bronchodilator — this is the key contrast with asthma (where reversibility is >12% + 200 mL).

Foundational — All Patients
  • Smoking cessation — the only intervention that meaningfully alters the disease course. First priority in all patients.
  • Pulmonary rehabilitation — improves exercise capacity, QoL and reduces hospital admissions
  • Annual influenza vaccine + one-off pneumococcal vaccine
  • BMI optimisation, nutrition, exercise

Add-On Therapies (Severe / Frequent Exacerbators)
Add-On Drug Options
  • Mucolytics (carbocisteine) — chronic productive cough; reduces sputum viscosity
  • Prophylactic azithromycin — frequent exacerbations (3+ per year); check ECG for QT prolongation + LFTs before starting
  • Oral theophylline — narrow therapeutic window; used only when inhaled therapy is insufficient
  • Roflumilast (PDE4 inhibitor) — severe COPD with chronic bronchitis + frequent exacerbations
LTOT — Long-Term Oxygen Therapy
  • PaO₂ <7.3 kPa on air → LTOT (at least 15 hrs/day)
  • PaO₂ 7.3–8 kPa + one of: polycythaemia, peripheral oedema, pulmonary HTN
  • NEVER in current smokers — fire risk; also assess compliance
  • Reduces pulmonary HTN progression + improves survival
Acute Exacerbation of COPD (AECOPD)
Triggers
  • Haemophilus influenzae — commonest bacterial trigger
  • Rhinovirus — commonest viral trigger
  • Streptococcus pneumoniae, Moraxella catarrhalis
  • Air pollution, cold weather
Features & Admission Criteria
  • Worsening breathlessness and cough
  • ↑ Sputum volume + colour change (purulence)
  • Admit if: unable to cope at home, severe symptoms, cyanosis, confusion, SpO₂ <90%, acidosis, significant comorbidity
Management of AECOPD
THE exam concept — Controlled Oxygen:
Target SpO₂ 88–92% in known/suspected CO₂ retainers via 28% Venturi mask.
CO₂ retainers may rely on hypoxic drive to breathe. Giving high-flow O₂ abolishes this drive → ↓respiratory rate → worsening hypercapnia → respiratory acidosis → arrest.
This is the single most-tested point in COPD.
🫁
Controlled O₂
28% Venturi mask → target SpO₂ 88–92%. Titrate up/down. Do NOT give high-flow unless SpO₂ <88% and recheck ABG.

RESPIRATORY__Tuberculosis:
Mycobacterium tuberculosis — acid-fast bacillus with upper-lobe predilection (high O₂ at apices favours growth). The organising thread: everything splits by latent vs active — it determines both testing and treatment. Disease arc: primary → latent → reactivation (secondary) → ± extrapulmonary / miliary.
Pathology & Natural History
Primary TB: inhaled bacilli → Ghon focus (lung parenchymal lesion) + ipsilateral hilar lymphadenopathy = Ghon complex. Histology: caseating granuloma — central caseous necrosis + epithelioid macrophages + Langhans giant cells. Mechanism: type IV hypersensitivity (cell-mediated).
Immunocompetent
Ghon focus heals & calcifies → latent TB: contained, asymptomatic, non-infectious. Reactivates if immunity wanes.
Immunocompromised
Failure to contain → haematogenous spread → miliary TB (disseminated "millet-seed" lesions in any organ).
Secondary (reactivation) TB: immunosuppression (HIV, steroids, malnutrition, age) reactivates dormant bacilli → lung apex → cavitation + haemoptysis.
Extrapulmonary sites — high-yield eponyms:
CNS → TB meningitis (most serious)  |  Spine → Pott's disease  |  Cervical nodes → scrofula  |  GI → ileocaecal TB  |  Renal → sterile pyuria
Risk Factors
Close contact with active TB High-prevalence origin (Asia, Africa, E Europe, Latin America) HIV / immunosuppression Homelessness / prison IVDU / alcohol excess Malnutrition Healthcare workers
Clinical Features
Primary TB
Usually asymptomatic. Occasionally erythema nodosum or mild flu-like illness.
Active / Reactivation TB
Systemic: fever, drenching night sweats, weight loss, malaise
Pulmonary: chronic productive cough (>3 wks), haemoptysis
Extrapulmonary
Site-specific: back pain (Pott's), neck lump (scrofula), meningism (TB meningitis), haematuria / sterile pyuria (renal)
Diagnosis
Latent TB Screening
Mantoux (Tuberculin Skin Test)
Intradermal PPD → read at 48–72 h; induration >5 mm = positive.
False negatives: miliary TB, HIV, sarcoid, lymphoma, very young, severe malnutrition, live vaccines
IGRA (Interferon-γ Release Assay)
Blood test measuring IFN-γ response to TB antigens. More specific than Mantoux — not affected by BCG vaccination. Preferred in BCG-vaccinated individuals.

RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Embolism and DVT:
VTE = DVT + PE — the same disease, two ends. Clot forms in the deep veins (usually legs) → embolises to the pulmonary arteries. PE is the a leading cause of direct maternal death and responsible for ~50% of post-operative deaths. Two diagnostic spines: Wells score → D-dimer/CTPA and the management fork: stable → anticoagulate / unstable → thrombolyse.
Pathophysiology & Virchow's Triad
Thrombus obstructs pulmonary artery
V/Q mismatch (ventilated but not perfused)
↑Pulmonary vascular resistance → acute right heart strain
Massive PE: RV failure → obstructive shock → arrest
Stasis
Immobility, long-haul flights, surgery, heart failure, paralysis, pregnancy
Endothelial Injury
Trauma, surgery, smoking, vasculitis, central lines
Hypercoagulability
Cancer (especially mucin-secreting), pregnancy, OCP/HRT, Factor V Leiden, thrombophilia, antiphospholipid syndrome, SLE, polycythaemia
Non-thrombotic emboli (rarer): fat (long-bone fracture) · air (central line, scuba) · amniotic fluid (obstetric emergency) · tumour
VTE Prophylaxis
All admissions: VTE risk-assess on admission LMWH (enoxaparin) — pharmacological Compression stockings / TED stockings — mechanical Early mobilisation
CI to LMWH: active bleeding, thrombocytopenia, acute stroke (haemorrhagic).  |  CI to stockings: PAD (peripheral arterial disease), severe leg oedema, neuropathy.
Clinical Features
Small / Medium PE
Pleuritic chest pain, breathlessness, haemoptysis, tachycardia, tachypnoea, low-grade fever, pleural rub
Massive PE
Central chest pain, shock / collapse, cyanosis, ↑JVP, RV heave, loud P2 or gallop rhythm — signs of acute right heart strain
DVT Signs
Unilateral leg — swelling, warmth, tenderness, erythema. Calf circumference >3cm difference = significant.
Classic Vignette
Post-op / long-haul flight patient + sudden SOB + pleuritic chest pain + tachycardia ± leg swelling
Diagnostic Algorithm
Wells 2-level PE score — key components: Clinical DVT signs (+3) · PE most likely diagnosis (+3) · Heart rate >100 (+1.5) · Immobilisation/surgery <4wks (+1.5) · Prior DVT/PE (+1.5) · Haemoptysis (+1) · Active malignancy (+1)

→ Immediate CTPA
Start interim anticoagulation if any delay
CTPA +ve → treat; CTPA −ve → consider leg USS
Wells ≤4 — PE Unlikely
→ D-dimer first
D-dimer −ve → stop, consider alternative diagnosis
D-dimer +ve → CTPA
Haemodynamically unstable and too sick for CTPA → bedside echo (RV dilatation = strong presumptive evidence) → thrombolyse empirically. Do not delay for imaging.

Deep Vein Thrombosis
Features
Unilateral leg — swelling, warmth, erythema, tenderness along vein. Calf circumference >3cm difference = significant. May have Homan's sign (unreliable — calf pain on dorsiflexion).
Diagnosis
2-level DVT Wells score → if likely: proximal leg USS (compression USS). If unlikely: D-dimer → USS if positive. Proximal DVT confirmed = treat as VTE.

Same as PE — DOAC first-line (apixaban/rivaroxaban); duration by provoked/unprovoked. Compression stockings for post-thrombotic prevention.
Complications
PE (embolisation — commonest serious complication); post-thrombotic syndrome (chronic venous insufficiency → leg pain, swelling, skin changes, ulcers)

RESPIRATORY__Pleural Effusion:
Excess fluid in the pleural space. Clinically detectable at >500 mL; visible on CXR at >300 mL. Massive effusion → think malignancy. The organising fork: transudate vs exudate — this single distinction drives investigation and management, decided by Light's criteria.
Transudate vs Exudate — The Spine
Transudate (<30 g/L protein) Exudate (>30 g/L protein)
Mechanism Pressure imbalance — ↑hydrostatic or ↓oncotic pressure pushes fluid across intact pleura Pleural damage / inflammation — ↑capillary permeability leaks protein-rich fluid
Causes Heart failure (commonest), hypoalbuminaemia (cirrhosis, nephrotic syndrome), hypothyroidism, Meigs syndrome Pneumonia (parapneumonic), malignancy, TB, PE, RA/connective tissue disease, pancreatitis, oesophageal rupture
Typical appearance Clear, straw-coloured; often bilateral Variable; may be turbid, purulent, bloody; usually unilateral
Memory hooks: Transudate = "the fluid is pushed across" (systemic disease, often bilateral)  |  Exudate = "the pleura is leaky" (local disease, inflammatory)
Light's Criteria
Used when protein is borderline (25–35 g/L). Classify as exudate if ANY ONE of these is met:
Criterion 1
Pleural fluid protein / serum protein > 0.5
Criterion 2
Pleural fluid LDH / serum LDH > 0.6
Criterion 3
Pleural fluid LDH > ⅔ of upper limit of normal serum LDH
Meet ANY one criterion = exudate. Must meet none of them to call transudate when borderline.
Clinical Features
Symptoms
Small → asymptomatic. Larger: progressive dyspnoea, pleuritic chest pain (exudates especially), dry cough
Examination — Key Signs
Stony dull percussion (distinguishes from consolidation which is dull)
Reduced/absent breath sounds
Reduced vocal fremitus/resonance
Reduced chest expansion ipsilaterally
Tracheal deviation away (massive effusion — mediastinal shift)
Effusion vs consolidation: both give dullness on percussion, but effusion = stony dull + absent breath sounds + reduced fremitus. Consolidation = dull + bronchial breathing + ↑vocal resonance.

CXRCostophrenic angle blunting (>300mL); meniscus sign; fluid in fissures; mediastinal shift (massive). Bilateral = transudate until proven otherwise.
USS chestConfirms fluid (vs consolidation); guides safe aspiration site; detects loculations
Diagnostic tap (USS-guided)First-line for undiagnosed exudate. Done in the triangle of safety (lateral chest, above rib, below axilla). Send: protein, LDH, glucose, pH, cytology, MC&S, ± amylase
CT thoraxIf aspiration non-diagnostic; pleural nodularity suggests malignancy; loculated collections
Pleural biopsyFor TB (Abrams needle) or malignancy (image-guided / thoracoscopic)
Fluid Appearance — Pattern Recognition:
Purulent → empyema Turbid → infection / inflammation Milky/creamy → chylothorax (thoracic duct leak) Bloodstained → haemothorax / malignancy Straw-coloured → transudate
Fluid biochemistry red flags: pH <7.2 + ↓glucose + ↑LDH → infected/complicated (needs drainage)  |  ↑amylase → pancreatitis or oesophageal rupture  |  cytology positive → malignancy

Management
Transudate
Treat the underlying cause — diurese heart failure, correct hypoalbuminaemia, treat hypothyroidism. Aspiration if tense/symptomatic.
Exudate
Treat underlying cause. Drainage if large/symptomatic (chest drain or aspiration). Send fluid for cytology/MC&S. Investigate for pneumonia, malignancy, TB.
Malignant Effusion
Recurs after aspiration. Drain to dryness then pleurodesis (talc instillation — sclerosant fuses pleural layers). Indwelling pleural catheter (IPC) for palliation if fails.
Small / Asymptomatic
Conservative management + monitoring. Serial USS/CXR. Investigate aetiology.

Parapneumonic Effusion & Empyema
The infective spectrum. Fluid analysis defines the stage and mandates the treatment — know the thresholds.
StageFluid CharacteristicsManagement
Simple parapneumonic Clear, sterile; normal pH (>7.2), normal glucose, normal LDH Antibiotics alone — resolves with treatment of pneumonia
Complicated parapneumonic Infected; pH <7.2, glucose <2.2 mmol/L, LDH >1000 Chest drain (intercostal) + antibiotics

Drain if: pH <7.2, glucose <2.2 mmol/L, LDH >1000, or frank pus. These three biochemical markers = the "empyema triad."
Haemothorax
Causes
Trauma (rib fractures → intercostal vessel injury) — commonest; malignancy; iatrogenic (central line, post-thoracic surgery)
Flail Segment
≥3 consecutive ribs fractured in ≥2 places → loss of chest wall rigidity → paradoxical movement (segment moves in on inspiration). Respiratory failure risk.
Management
A–E resuscitation; tranexamic acid (TXA) early; large-bore chest drain (28–40Fr) — prevents clotting/empyema. VATS within 48–72h if >500mL drained or ongoing bleeding. Massive → thoracotomy.

RESPIRATORY__Pneumothorax:
Air in the pleural space → partial or complete lung collapse. The framing: classify (primary vs secondary) → manage by size + symptoms → never miss tension (the emergency). Cross-ref pleural effusion — same pleural space, same triangle of safety and chest drain technique; the key contrast is hyperresonant (pneumothorax) vs stony dull (effusion).
Classification & Aetiology
Primary Spontaneous
No underlying lung disease. Tall, thin, young men; ruptured subpleural bleb/bulla. Smoking is a risk factor. Good prognosis — manage conservatively if small.
Secondary Spontaneous
Underlying lung disease — COPD (commonest), asthma, CF, bronchiectasis, TB, malignancy. Worse outcomes — lower threshold to drain; admit all.
Traumatic / Iatrogenic
Rib fractures, biopsy, central line insertion, mechanical ventilation (barotrauma), chest drain complications
Tension Pneumothorax
Emergency subtype — one-way valve mechanism → progressive pressure build-up. Can occur from any cause. See dedicated section below.
Clinical Features
Symptoms
Sudden onset pleuritic chest pain ± breathlessness. May be minimal in primary (small). Marked dyspnoea in secondary (limited reserve).
Examination — Air Signature

Tension Pneumothorax — The Emergency
Clinical diagnosis only — do NOT wait for CXR. Treat immediately or patient will arrest.
Mechanism
One-way valve: air enters pleura on inspiration but cannot escape → progressive ↑intrapleural pressure → mediastinal shift → kinked great vessels → obstructive shock → cardiac arrest
Clinical Signs
Tracheal deviation AWAY from affected side
↓air entry + hyperresonance on affected side
Distended neck veins
Tachycardia → hypotension → arrest
Severe respiratory distress
Immediate Management
1. Needle decompression (emergency): large-bore cannula (14G), 2nd ICS, midclavicular line (or 5th ICS, mid-axillary line per updated ATLS) → hiss of air confirms

Triangle of Safety
Bounded by: lateral border of pectoralis major (anterior) · anterior border of latissimus dorsi (posterior) · 5th ICS / nipple line (inferior) · apex of axilla (superior). Always insert above the rib (neurovascular bundle runs below).
Underwater Seal
Acts as a one-way valve: air/fluid exits, cannot re-enter. Swinging with respiration = correctly sited. Bubbling = active air leak. No swing = blocked or drain displaced.

Never lift the bottle above the patient → retrograde flow back into pleura
Never clamp a bubbling drain → tension pneumothorax
Swinging = good; no swing = re-examine/reposition

RESPIRATORY__Cystic Fibrosis:
Autosomal recessive — CFTR gene, chromosome 7 — defective cAMP-regulated Cl⁻ channel. Commonest mutation: ΔF508. The mechanism that explains everything: defective Cl⁻ (and water) transport → thick, viscous secretions → blocked tubes in every exocrine organ. One channel defect → multi-system disease: lungs, pancreas, gut, reproductive tract.

Airway surface in cystic fibrosis. The normal airway (left) maintains a hydrated surface liquid layer and effective mucociliary clearance, whereas the CF airway (right) shows defective CFTR function → reduced airway surface liquid, impaired clearance, and thick, excessive mucus.

© Abraham Zakik, Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0

Pathophysiology
CFTR mutation → defective Cl⁻ channel
Impaired Cl⁻ & water secretion onto epithelial surfaces
Dehydrated, thick, viscous mucus
Obstruction of airways, pancreatic ducts, bile ducts, vas deferens…
Recurrent infections, malabsorption, infertility, organ damage
Every feature in this condition traces back to this single mechanism — a tube blocked by thick secretions.
Clinical Features
Respiratory
Thick airway mucus → impaired mucociliary clearance → recurrent infections → bronchiectasis, clubbing, nasal polyps, sinusitis
GI / Pancreatic
Blocked pancreatic ducts → exocrine insufficiency → malabsorption, steatorrhoea, failure to thrive; fat-soluble vitamin deficiency (ADEK); CF-related diabetes; biliary → cirrhosis
Neonatal
Meconium ileus — classic newborn presentation (intestinal obstruction); prolonged neonatal jaundice; failure to pass meconium
Reproductive
Male infertility — bilateral absence of vas deferens (azoospermia); female subfertility (thick cervical mucus)
Other
Rectal prolapse (bulky stools), short stature, delayed puberty, salt-loss in heat / exercise

OrganismContext / Significance
Staphylococcus aureusEarly / childhood coloniser — most common initially
Pseudomonas aeruginosaLater coloniser — marker of disease progression; very difficult to eradicate; treat with nebulised tobramycin / oral ciprofloxacin
Burkholderia cepaciaThe dangerous one — associated with rapid decline; contraindicates lung transplant
Aspergillus fumigatusCan cause allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis (ABPA) — treat with steroids ± itraconazole

Sweat Test — Gold Standard
Pilocarpine iontophoresis → sweat chloride >60 mmol/L = positive (normal <40). Repeat if borderline (40–60).
False positives: skin oedema, malnutrition, adrenal insufficiency

Heel-prick — immunoreactive trypsinogen (IRT); if elevated → confirm with genetic testing. Part of UK newborn screening programme.
Genetic Testing
CFTR mutation analysis — confirms diagnosis, identifies ΔF508 and other mutations; guides eligibility for modulators
Other
Spirometry (obstructive pattern), CXR / HRCT (bronchiectasis, hyperinflation), sputum cultures (track colonisation), HbA1c / OGTT (CF-related diabetes), LFTs
Management
MDT approach: respiratory physician, physiotherapist, dietitian, specialist CF nurse, gastroenterologist, endocrinologist, fertility specialist, psychologist
Respiratory
Chest physio + postural drainage (≥2×/day) Nebulised DNase (dornase alfa) — thins mucus Prophylactic antibiotics Pseudomonas → nebulised tobramycin / oral ciprofloxacin Bronchodilators, hypertonic saline
Nutritional
High-calorie, high-fat diet Pancreatic enzyme replacement (Creon) with every meal Fat-soluble vitamins ADEK supplementation Manage CF-related diabetes (insulin)
CFTR Modulators
Lumacaftor / Ivacaftor (Orkambi)
For ΔF508 homozygotes. Lumacaftor = corrector (folds CFTR correctly); Ivacaftor = potentiator (keeps channel open). Increases functional CFTR at cell surface — disease-modifying.
Elexacaftor / Tezacaftor / Ivacaftor (Kaftrio)
Triple therapy — highly effective for ΔF508 (one or two copies). Significantly improves lung function, reduces exacerbations.
Advanced / Other
Lung transplant (bilateral) — NOT if chronic Burkholderia cepacia Genetic counselling — AR; 25% risk in siblings Carrier screening for partners
Burkholderia cepacia = absolute contraindication to lung transplant.

RESPIRATORY__Sarcoidosis:
Multisystem granulomatous disorder of unknown cause. The defining lesion: non-caseating granuloma (epithelioid cells + multinucleate giant cells) — the word non-caseating is the key contrast with TB (which is caseating). Epidemiology: young/middle-aged adults, F > M, more common and more severe in Black patients, northern European. Commonest presentation: bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy (BHL); ~50% found incidentally on CXR.

Pathology & Immunology
Granuloma Composition
Non-caseating granuloma = focal epithelioid macrophages, multinucleate giant cells, CD4+ T cells. No central necrosis — the absence of caseation is the defining feature.
BAL & Lymphocyte Paradox
↑CD4 T cells in BAL (CD4:CD8 ratio ↑ in active disease). Paradoxically: peripheral lymphopenia + cutaneous anergy — lymphocytes are sequestered in granulomas, depressing tuberculin/Candida skin test reactivity.
Hypercalcaemia Mechanism
Activated macrophages in granulomas produce 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D₃ (calcitriol) → unregulated ↑Ca²⁺ absorption → hypercalcaemia ± hypercalciuria. Explains the metabolic feature without primary hyperparathyroidism.

SystemFeatures
Chest (commonest)Dry cough, breathlessness, fine crackles; BHL ± pulmonary infiltrates; often asymptomatic
SkinErythema nodosum (acute, tender nodules, shins); lupus pernio (indurated violaceous plaques on nose/cheeks — most specific sign); scar infiltration
EyesUveitis (anterior most common — red eye, photophobia, floaters); lacrimal gland enlargement; conjunctival nodules
MetabolicHypercalcaemia (macrophage 1,25-D₃ production) → polyuria, constipation, renal stones
Bone / JointArthralgia, periarthritis, bone cysts (hands/feet)
LiverGranulomatous hepatitis, hepatosplenomegaly, ↑ALP
NeurologyCranial nerve palsy (especially CN VII — facial palsy), meningeal involvement, pituitary/hypothalamic infiltration, peripheral neuropathy
Cardiac (rare but dangerous)Conduction defects (heart block), arrhythmias, cardiomyopathy — can cause sudden death

BHL + erythema nodosum + polyarthralgia (± fever). Acute onset. Good prognosis — spontaneously resolves in most. Classic SBA name: "which syndrome is associated with a good outcome?"

Uveitis + parotid gland enlargement + facial nerve palsy (CN VII) + fever. Subacute onset. More chronic course than Löfgren's. Think: eye + parotid + face.
Differentials of Bilateral Hilar Lymphadenopathy
Sarcoidosis (commonest) Lymphoma Tuberculosis Bronchial carcinoma with nodal spread Infections (EBV, fungi)
Symmetrical BHL + erythema nodosum = essentially only sarcoidosis — this combination is near-pathognomonic and rarely needs biopsy to confirm.

RESPIRATORY__Anaphylaxis:
Overview

Anaphylaxis is a severe type 1 (IgE-mediated) hypersensitivity reaction → mast cell degranulation → histamine release → airway / breathing / circulation compromise. Rapid onset is the hallmark.

Common Triggers
  • Foods — nuts, shellfish, egg, milk
  • Insect venom — bee/wasp stings
  • Drugs — penicillins, NSAIDs, contrast media
  • Latex
  • Idiopathic
The Framing

This is an emergency. The entire management reduces to:

Recognition → IM adrenaline

Everything else is adjunctive.

Recognition — What Makes It Anaphylaxis
Anaphylaxis = acute onset + life-threatening A/B/C compromise, usually with skin changes.
Skin changes alone (urticaria, angioedema) without A/B/C = allergic reaction, not anaphylaxis.
🫁
Airway
Swelling, hoarseness, stridor — upper airway oedema threatening occlusion
💨
Breathing
SOB, wheeze (bronchospasm), hypoxia, increasing respiratory fatigue
❤️
Circulation
Hypotension, tachycardia, collapse, light-headedness, pallor
🌸
Skin (usually present, NOT required alone)
Urticaria, itching, flushing, angioedema (lips, tongue, eyes)
Management — The Algorithm
IM ADRENALINE IS THE FIRST AND MOST IMPORTANT ACTION — give before antihistamines and steroids.
💉
IM Adrenaline 1:1000 — anterolateral thigh (middle third)
Adult: 500 mcg (0.5 mL). Repeat after 5 minutes if no improvement. IM not IV — IV is specialist-only (arrhythmia risk).
🅾️
A/B — Airway + Breathing
Secure airway (call anaesthetics early if stridor). High-flow O₂ via non-rebreathe. Salbutamol nebuliser if wheeze.
🩸
C — Circulation
IV access; IV fluid bolus (500–1000 mL crystalloid adult; 10 mL/kg child). Monitor ECG and BP.
🛏️
D — Position
Lie flat + raise legs (improves venous return and cerebral perfusion). Sit up only if breathing is the dominant problem.
💊
Adjuncts — after adrenaline, NOT instead of
Antihistamine (chlorphenamine/cetirizine) · IV hydrocortisone 200 mg. NB: current guidance de-emphasises steroids/antihistamines as acute treatment — adrenaline is the priority.

>12 years / adult500 mcg0.5 mL
Refractory Anaphylaxis

Defined: respiratory/cardiovascular compromise persisting despite 2 IM adrenaline doses.

  • Continue IV fluid resuscitation (adults 500–1000 mL; children 10 mL/kg boluses)
  • Senior/expert help immediately
  • IV adrenaline infusion — specialist/ITU only (arrhythmia risk requires monitoring)
  • Consider intubation if airway deteriorating
After the Event
Immediate Post-Acute
  • Serum mast cell tryptase — within 6 hours of onset (confirms mast cell degranulation; serial samples ideal at 0, 1–2 h, >24 h)
  • Observation period — risk of biphasic reaction (recurrence hours later without re-exposure)
  • Non-sedating antihistamine for persisting skin symptoms
Discharge Planning
  • Two adrenaline auto-injectors prescribed (EpiPen/Jext) + technique demonstrated
  • Allergy clinic referral (all new diagnoses)
  • Written action plan + trigger avoidance advice
  • Medical alert bracelet (Medic-Alert) discussion

Biphasic reaction — observe before discharge
2 auto-injectors + allergy referral on discharge

RESPIRATORY__Pulmonary Hypertension:
PH = ↑pulmonary arterial pressure (mean PAP >20 mmHg) → right heart pressure overload → cor pulmonale → systemic venous congestion. Classified into 5 WHO groups by cause — the spine of this topic. The mechanistic thread: every feature (ECG, CXR, signs) = the right heart struggling against high pulmonary resistance.
WHO Classification — 5 Groups
GroupCauseExamples
1 — PAH Pulmonary arterial hypertension (primary vascular) Idiopathic; connective tissue disease (scleroderma, SLE); congenital heart disease (Eisenmenger); HIV; drugs (fenfluramine)
2 — Left heart Left heart disease — commonest cause overall LV failure, mitral/aortic valve disease, systemic hypertension
3 — Lung/hypoxia Chronic lung disease / hypoxia-driven vasoconstriction COPD (commonest in this group), ILD, OSA, high altitude
4 — CTEPH Chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension Recurrent / inadequately treated PE → organised clot → obstructed vessels
5 — Misc Multifactorial / unclear mechanisms Sarcoidosis, haematological disorders (sickle cell), metabolic, compression of pulmonary vessels
Two to anchor: Group 2 (left heart disease) = commonest cause overall. Group 1 (PAH) = the one with specific pulmonary vasodilator drug therapy.
Pathophysiology
↑Pulmonary vascular resistance (any cause)
RV pressure overload → RV hypertrophy
RV failure (cor pulmonale)
Back-pressure → systemic venous congestion (↑JVP, oedema, hepatomegaly)
This single chain explains every sign, ECG change, and CXR finding in PH.
Clinical Features
Early Symptoms
Exertional dyspnoea (main presenting symptom), fatigue, exertional syncope (fixed low cardiac output — cannot augment with exercise), chest pain
Advanced / Cor Pulmonale
Raised JVP, peripheral oedema, hepatomegaly (± pulsatile liver), ascites, pleural effusion
Clinical Signs
Loud P2 (pulmonary valve closure), RV heave (parasternal), tricuspid regurgitation murmur (pansystolic, LSE, louder on inspiration)
Exertional syncope = fixed low output — the RV cannot increase output on demand (obstructed outflow). A high-yield clinical clue to PH.
Investigations
TestFinding / Role
ECGRVH (dominant R in V1–3, deep S in V5–6); right axis deviation; RBBB; P pulmonale (peaked P in II — RA enlargement)
CXRDilated proximal pulmonary arteries tapering distally ("pruning"); RV/RA enlargement; peripheral oligaemia
NT-proBNP↑ — right heart strain marker; correlates with severity and prognosis
Echo — key screening testEstimates pulmonary artery pressure (via TR jet velocity); RV size/function; excludes left heart disease (Group 2); guides referral
Right heart catheterisation — gold standardDirect measurement of PAP and pulmonary vascular resistance; confirms diagnosis; vasoreactivity testing (to guide CCB therapy in Group 1)
PFTsIdentify Group 3 (obstructive/restrictive lung disease)
CTPA / V-Q scanIdentify Group 4 (CTEPH — organised thrombus)
Autoantibodies (ANA, anti-Scl-70, anti-dsDNA)Identify connective tissue disease (Group 1 — scleroderma, SLE)
Management
Principle: treat the underlying cause first (by WHO group). PAH-specific vasodilator drugs are for Group 1 only — not for other groups.
Treat the Cause (by group)
Group 2 → treat the left heart (diuretics, ACEi, valve surgery)
Group 3 → treat COPD/ILD + LTOT (↓hypoxic vasoconstriction)
Group 4 → anticoagulate + pulmonary endarterectomy (potentially curative for CTEPH)
Supportive (all groups)
O₂ (especially Group 3); diuretics (peripheral oedema/ascites); anticoagulation (thrombosis risk in Group 1/4); avoid pregnancy; supervised exercise
PAH-Specific Therapy (Group 1)
Reduce pulmonary vascular resistance:
Prostanoids — epoprostenol (IV), iloprost (inhaled)
Endothelin receptor antagonists (ERAs) — bosentan, macitentan
PDE-5 inhibitors — sildenafil, tadalafil
CCBs — only if vasoreactive on right heart catheter testing
End-Stage
Lung or heart-lung transplant — for refractory Group 1 PAH or Group 4 CTEPH not suitable for endarterectomy
⭐ Exam Pearls
5 WHO groups: 1=PAH (CTD/idiopathic) · 2=left heart (commonest) · 3=lung/hypoxia (COPD) · 4=CTEPH (chronic PE) · 5=misc
Mechanism: ↑pulmonary pressure → RV strain → cor pulmonale → systemic congestion. Every sign traces to this chain.
ECG: RVH + right axis deviation + RBBB + P pulmonale — all signs of right heart strain
CXR: dilated proximal pulmonary arteries tapering distally ("pruning") + RV/RA enlargement
Echo = screening (estimates PAP). Right heart catheter = gold standard (direct PAP measurement + vasoreactivity testing).
Treat the cause first. PAH-specific drugs (sildenafil, ERAs, prostanoids) = Group 1 only — don't use in Group 2 (can worsen LV failure).
Loud P2 + exertional syncope = classic PH exam vignette. Syncope = fixed low output.
Group 4 (CTEPH): anticoagulate + consider pulmonary endarterectomy — potentially curative. Cross-ref PE.
Group 3 (COPD): LTOT reduces hypoxic vasoconstriction — the primary Group 3 intervention
Scleroderma (systemic sclerosis) = highest PAH risk among CTDs — screen annually with echo
RESPIRATORY__Obstructive Sleep Apnoea:
Repeated pharyngeal airway collapse during sleep → apnoeas (≥10 sec cessation) → recurrent micro-arousals + intermittent hypoxia. Classic patient: overweight, middle-aged man (also children with enlarged tonsils). Two consequence streams: sleep fragmentation → daytime symptoms and intermittent hypoxia → cardiovascular risk.
Pathophysiology
Sleep → pharyngeal dilator muscles become hypotonic
Airway sucked closed on inspiration → apnoea
Struggle to breathe → brief arousal (patient unaware; hundreds per night)
Airway reopens → cycle repeats throughout night
Stream 1 — Sleep Fragmentation
Hundreds of micro-arousals → never reaches deep restorative sleep → excessive daytime sleepiness, poor concentration, mood change, morning headache
Stream 2 — Intermittent Hypoxia
Repeated desaturations → sympathetic activation → hypertension (especially resistant), ↑MI/stroke risk, arrhythmias (AF), cor pulmonale
Risk Factors
Obesity (biggest modifiable RF) Male sex Middle age Large neck circumference Enlarged tonsils / adenoids (children) Retrognathia / craniofacial abnormality Alcohol / sedatives (↑muscle relaxation) Smoking Hypothyroidism Acromegaly
Clinical Features
Nocturnal (often partner-reported)
Loud snoring, witnessed apnoeas, nocturnal choking / gasping, restless sleep, nocturia
Daytime
Excessive daytime sleepiness (falling asleep driving, in meetings), unrefreshing sleep, morning headache, poor concentration, personality change, low libido
Consequences (severe / untreated)
Resistant hypertension, cor pulmonale / right heart failure, AF, ↑MI / stroke risk, type 2 diabetes worsening, road traffic accidents
Investigations
Epworth Sleepiness Scale — Screening
Patient rates likelihood of dozing in 8 everyday situations (0–3 each; max 24). >10 = excessive daytime sleepiness → warrants investigation. Differentiates OSA from simple snoring.
Sleep Study (Polysomnography) — Diagnostic
Gold standard. Measures sleep stages, airflow, oxygen saturation, respiratory effort, EEG, ECG. Gives the Apnoea-Hypopnoea Index (AHI) = events per hour.
Home Oximetry
Overnight pulse oximetry — frequent desaturations (saw-tooth pattern) is suggestive. Simpler and cheaper; used for initial screening or where polysomnography unavailable.
AHI (events/hour)Severity
<5Normal
5–14Mild OSA
15–29Moderate OSA
≥30Severe OSA
Management
Conservative (all patients)
Weight loss — most important modifiable factor; can resolve mild OSA. Avoid alcohol and sedatives (↑muscle relaxation). Smoking cessation. Sleep position (lateral). Treat hypothyroidism/acromegaly if present.
CPAP — Mainstay for Moderate/Severe
Continuous Positive Airway Pressure — tight nasal/full-face mask delivers continuous positive pressure to pneumatically splint the upper airway open. Used every night. Dramatically improves sleepiness, BP, and cardiovascular outcomes.
Mandibular Advancement Device
Oral appliance that protrudes the lower jaw → opens oropharyngeal space. For mild OSA, simple snorers, or CPAP-intolerant patients.
Surgery
Tonsillectomy (children with enlarged tonsils — often curative). UPPP (uvulopalatopharyngoplasty) — resects uvula/soft palate; variable results in adults.
DVLA notification is mandatory — patients with excessive daytime sleepiness must inform the DVLA and must not drive while sleepy. Group 2 licence (HGV/bus) = immediate notification. Medicolegally important.
⭐ Exam Pearls
Apnoea = ≥10 sec cessation. Severity by AHI: mild 5–14 · moderate 15–29 · severe ≥30.
Classic vignette: obese middle-aged man + loud snoring + partner witnesses apnoeas + daytime sleepiness
Epworth >10 = abnormal (screening tool). Polysomnography = diagnostic gold standard.
CPAP = mainstay for moderate-severe. Mandibular advancement device for mild / CPAP-intolerant.
Weight loss = most important modifiable factor. Avoid alcohol and sedatives (worsen pharyngeal collapse).
Must inform DVLA; do not drive when sleepy. HGV/bus licence = immediate notification.
Cardiovascular consequences: resistant hypertension (think OSA in any patient with poorly controlled BP), AF, ↑MI/stroke, cor pulmonale
Cross-ref: OSA = Group 3 cause of pulmonary hypertension (hypoxia-driven vasoconstriction → cor pulmonale)
RESPIRATORY__Smoking Cessation:
NICE recommends offering NRT, varenicline, or bupropion alongside behavioural support to all smokers who want to quit. Three pharmacological options (a comparison) + one special case: pregnancy (different rules apply). The universal cross-topic intervention — appears in COPD, IHD, lung cancer, PAD, OSA, and stroke prevention.
The Three Agents — Comparison Table
NRT Varenicline (Champix) Bupropion (Zyban)
Mechanism Nicotine replacement — reduces withdrawal symptoms Nicotinic receptor partial agonist — reduces craving (agonist) + blocks nicotine reward (antagonist) Noradrenaline/dopamine reuptake inhibitor + nicotinic antagonist — reduces craving and withdrawal
When to start At quit date 1 week before quit date; continue for 12 weeks 1–2 weeks before quit date
Key side effects Nausea, headache, flu-like, local irritation (patch/gum) Nausea (commonest), insomnia, vivid/abnormal dreams, mood change Seizures (most important), insomnia, dry mouth, headache
Cautions / CI Caution in acute MI, unstable angina; remove patch before sleep if vivid dreams Caution: depression / history of self-harm; CI: pregnancy and breastfeeding CI: epilepsy (lowers seizure threshold); CI: pregnancy and breastfeeding; eating disorders, bipolar
Three distinguishing hooks: Varenicline = partial agonist + vivid dreams + mood caution  |  Bupropion = seizure risk + CI in epilepsy  |  NRT = combine patch + fast-acting for high dependence
NRT — Forms & Combination Therapy
Long-Acting (Baseline)
Transdermal patch (16h or 24h) — steady background level. 24h patch: remove before sleep if causing insomnia or vivid dreams.
Short-Acting (Craving Relief)
Gum, lozenge, nasal spray, inhalator, sublingual tablet — faster absorption to manage acute cravings
Combination for High Dependence
Patch + short-acting agent — patch provides baseline nicotine, short-acting covers breakthrough cravings. More effective than either alone in highly dependent smokers.
Pregnancy — The Special Case
Varenicline and bupropion are absolutely contraindicated in pregnancy and breastfeeding.
Step 1 — Objective Screening
CO (carbon monoxide) testing at every antenatal appointment — patients often under-report smoking. CO >4 ppm = active smoker. Objective, non-judgmental.
Step 2 — Behavioural Support (First-line)
CBT and motivational interviewing — first-line in pregnancy. Refer to specialist stop-smoking service.
Step 3 — NRT (Second-line)
NRT if behavioural support alone insufficient. Remove 16h patch before sleeping. Safer than continuing to smoke.
Pregnancy rule: behavioural first → NRT if needed → never varenicline or bupropion
⭐ Exam Pearls
Varenicline = nicotinic partial agonist. Start 1 week before quit date. Key SEs: vivid dreams + mood/behaviour change. Caution in depression/self-harm history.
Bupropion = seizure risk. CI in epilepsy (and eating disorders, bipolar). Start 1–2 weeks before quit date.
Both varenicline and bupropion: CI in pregnancy and breastfeeding.
Pregnancy: CBT/motivational interviewing first → NRT second (remove patch before sleep) → no varenicline/bupropion ever. Use CO testing to screen objectively.
Combination NRT (patch + short-acting) for high dependence — more effective than monotherapy
All pharmacotherapy starts before the quit date (varenicline 1 wk, bupropion 1–2 wks) to reach therapeutic effect
The universal intervention: smoking cessation appears in COPD, IHD, lung cancer, PAD, OSA, stroke prevention — always mention it

Nodules coalesce → large upper-lobe fibrotic masses (>1 cm). Features: black sputum (melanoptysis), progressive dyspnoea, mixed obstructive/restrictive PFTs, cor pulmonale in advanced disease.

Remove from exposure; smoking cessation (↓COPD progression); supportive (inhaled bronchodilators, O₂); no specific treatment; compensable (IIDB).
Silicosis
Inhalation of crystalline silica → macrophage activation → fibrotic nodule formation. Upper-zone disease. The most important risk is reactivation TB — silica impairs macrophage killing of mycobacteria.

Sandblasting (highest risk), stone quarrying, slate working, pottery, foundries, tunnelling, glass manufacturing

Remove from exposure; screen and treat latent TB; supportive care; no disease-modifying treatment; compensable (IIDB)
Always screen silicosis patients for TB — Mantoux/IGRA + CXR. Silicosis + TB = silicotuberculosis, rapid deterioration.

Bronchiectasis is permanent, irreversible dilatation of bronchi → impaired secretion clearance → recurrent infection and inflammation. Unlike COPD (obstruction) or asthma (reversible narrowing), bronchiectasis is defined by dilated, mucus-pooling airways.

The spine: Everything in bronchiectasis — why sputum is copious, why it progresses, and why management targets clearance and infection — is explained by the vicious cycle.

High-Yield Named Causes
  • Kartagener's syndrome — immotile cilia (primary ciliary dyskinesia) + situs inversus + sinusitis
  • ABPA (allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis) — asthmatic + Aspergillus allergy → central bronchiectasis
  • Immunodeficiency — HIV, hypogammaglobulinaemia (check Ig levels)
  • Obstruction — foreign body, enlarged TB lymph nodes (e.g. in children)
Clinical Features
Symptoms
  • Chronic cough + copious purulent sputum — the cardinal feature
  • Recurrent chest infections
  • Haemoptysis — can be massive and life-threatening (eroded bronchial artery)
  • Progressive breathlessness, wheeze, fatigue
Examination
  • Coarse crackles — typically at the bases (or wherever disease is located)
  • Clubbing (chronic suppurative lung disease)
  • Wheeze (from airway oedema)
  • Signs of cor pulmonale in advanced disease
Investigations
🖥️
HRCT Chest — Gold Standard
Signet ring sign: airway lumen wider than its accompanying artery. Bronchial wall thickening, lack of airway tapering, mucus plugging, cysts.
🩻
CXR
May be normal or show "tramtrack" lines (thickened parallel bronchial walls). Insensitive — HRCT always needed to confirm.
🧫
Sputum MC&S
Essential in exacerbation. Common organisms: H. influenzae (commonest), Pseudomonas aeruginosa (persistent green sputum), S. aureus.
🧬
Cause Workup
Immunoglobulins (hypogammaglobulinaemia) · Sweat test (CF) · Aspergillus serology/IgE (ABPA) · Nasal ciliary biopsy (Kartagener's)

Management — Break the Vicious Cycle
Airway Clearance — Mainstay (targets the mucus arm)
  • Chest physiotherapy — active cycle of breathing technique (ACBT), postural drainage
  • Oscillatory PEP devices — Flutter / Acapella (vibration loosens mucus)
  • Mucolytics (hypertonic saline nebulisation)
  • Regular, daily — not just during exacerbations
Treat / Prevent Infection (targets the infection arm)
  • Prompt antibiotics for exacerbations (↑cough, ↑sputum volume, purulence)
  • S. aureus → flucloxacillin
  • Persistent green sputum → Pseudomonas → dual therapy (e.g. ciprofloxacin + another agent)
  • Prophylactic azithromycin (≥3 exacerbations/year) — check ECG (QT) + LFTs first
Supportive / Other
  • Smoking cessation
  • Flu + pneumococcal vaccines
  • Bronchodilators if dyspnoeic
  • Treat underlying cause (CF, ABPA, immunodeficiency)
  • Surgery — localised resectable disease or end-stage transplant
Complications
  • Massive haemoptysis — life-threatening
  • Pneumonia, empyema
  • Pneumothorax
  • Respiratory failure
  • Cor pulmonale
  • Metastatic abscess (e.g. cerebral)
  • Non-TB mycobacteria colonisation
  • Aspergillus colonisation / ABPA
⭐ Exam Pearls
HRCT = gold standard; signs = signet ring (dilated airway > artery) + tramtracks (CXR)
Cardinal feature: copious purulent sputum + chronic cough + clubbing
Commonest cause = post-infectious (ask about childhood LRTIs); CF the key genetic cause
Commonest organism = H. influenzae; persistent green sputum → Pseudomonas → dual antibiotics
Kartagener's = immotile cilia + situs inversus + sinusitis
ABPA = asthmatic + Aspergillus allergy → central bronchiectasis
Mainstay = airway clearance physio + treat infection (break the vicious cycle)
Azithromycin prophylaxis if ≥3 exacerbations/yr — check QT + LFTs first

RESPIRATORY__Acute Bronchitis:
Overview

Acute bronchitis is a self-limiting lower respiratory tract infection (LRTI) — inflammation of the trachea and major bronchi → oedematous large airways + increased sputum. Usually viral. Resolves in <3 weeks.

Two things matter: (1) distinguish from pneumonia and (2) apply the CRP-guided antibiotic decision. Most cases are managed supportively.
Anatomy Overview
Clinical Features
Symptoms
  • Cough — dominant symptom; may or may not be productive
  • Sore throat, rhinorrhoea
  • Wheeze (from airway inflammation)
  • Low-grade or no fever
  • Systemic features (malaise, myalgia) often absent
Examination
  • Chest exam normally CLEAR — the key finding
  • ± Mild wheeze; ± low-grade fever
  • No focal chest signs — no dullness, no bronchial breathing, no crackles
Bronchitis vs Pneumonia
Feature Acute Bronchitis Pneumonia
Chest exam Usually normal Focal signs — dullness, bronchial breathing, ↓BS, crackles
Systemic features Often absent Present — fever, rigors, malaise, myalgia
CXR Normal (not routinely needed) Consolidation ± air bronchograms
Course Self-limiting <3 weeks Needs antibiotic treatment
Exam line: Clear chest + no systemic upset = bronchitis. Focal signs + systemic illness = pneumonia.
Management — CRP-Guided Antibiotic Decision

Supportive care is the mainstay — analgesia, fluids, reassurance that it is self-limiting.

Situation / CRP Action
Systemically unwell / significant comorbidities Consider antibiotics regardless of CRP
CRP <20 mg/L No antibiotic
CRP 20–100 mg/L Delayed / back-up prescription
CRP >100 mg/L Immediate antibiotic
Antibiotic Choice
  • First-line: doxycycline — 200 mg day 1, then 100 mg OD × 4 days
  • Doxycycline CONTRAINDICATED in children & pregnancy → use amoxicillin instead
⭐ Exam Pearls
Clear chest + no systemic features = bronchitis (vs pneumonia's focal signs)
Usually viral, self-limiting <3 weeks — antibiotics often not needed
CRP <20 → none / 20–100 → delayed / >100 → immediate
Doxycycline first-line; amoxicillin in children & pregnancy
Mostly supportive — do not over-treat

RESPIRATORY__Respiratory and Oxygen Supp:
Respiratory support follows an escalation ladder: oxygen → high-flow nasal cannula → non-invasive ventilation → mechanical ventilation → ECMO. Two anchors examined most: oxygen saturation targets (which patient gets what %) and the CPAP vs BiPAP distinction (Type 1 vs Type 2 respiratory failure).
The Escalation Ladder
Supplemental O₂
Nasal cannula / mask / NRB / Venturi
High-Flow Nasal Cannula (HFNC)
Up to 60 L/min + gentle PEEP
NIV — CPAP / BiPAP
Type 1 (CPAP) / Type 2 (BiPAP)
Invasive Mechanical Ventilation
ETT + sedation
ECMO
Specialist centres; reversible failure
Oxygen Targets — Highest-Yield Point
Most Acutely Ill Patients
Target SpO₂ 94–98%. Titrate O₂ to achieve and maintain this range.
CO₂ Retainers (COPD, Type 2 RF)
Target SpO₂ 88–92% via 28% Venturi mask at 4 L/min. Controlled oxygen prevents blunting of hypoxic drive → avoids worsening hypercapnia. Drive nebulisers with air, not O₂.
Critically Ill (Shock, Arrest, Anaphylaxis)
Start 15 L/min via non-rebreather mask — hypoxia kills acutely. Titrate down once stabilised. Never withhold O₂ in a crashing patient.
Rule: High-flow O₂ in the critically ill. Controlled O₂ in CO₂ retainers (COPD) — the single most examined O₂ prescribing point.
Oxygen Delivery Devices
DeviceFiO₂FlowKey Notes
Nasal cannula 24–44% ≤4 L/min Comfortable; patient can talk/eat; variable FiO₂ (affected by breathing pattern)
Simple face mask (Hudson) 40–60% 5–10 L/min Mild-moderate hypoxia; variable FiO₂; must run ≥5L (avoid CO₂ re-breathing)
Non-rebreather mask (reservoir) 60–95% 15 L/min Severe/critically ill; variable FiO₂ (entrains some air); highest O₂ delivery without intubation
