Venturi = fixed performance (precise FiO₂) — the only device that guarantees a known inspired O₂ concentration. All others are variable performance.
PEEP — The Unifying Concept
Prevents alveolar collapse at end-expiration ↓Atelectasis Improves oxygenation ↓Work of breathing Recruits collapsed lung units
Added by: HFNC (small amount), CPAP/BiPAP (controlled), mechanical ventilator (precise titration)
High-Flow Nasal Cannula (HFNC)
How It Works
Delivers up to 60 L/min of warmed, humidified oxygen via wide-bore nasal prongs. Generates low-level PEEP, washes out nasopharyngeal dead space, reduces work of breathing.
Role
Bridge between standard O₂ and NIV — for patients failing standard O₂ who aren't yet in Type 2 failure. Well-tolerated, allows talking and eating. Mainly for Type 1 respiratory failure.
Non-Invasive Ventilation — CPAP vs BiPAP
CPAPBiPAP
Pressure Constant single pressure throughout breathing cycle Two pressures — higher iPAP (inspiration) + lower ePAP (expiration)
Action Splints airways and alveoli open; improves oxygenation; reduces work of breathing Actively assists ventilation — iPAP supports inspiration → ↓CO₂, ↑tidal volume
Failure type Type 1 RF (↓O₂, normal CO₂) Type 2 RF (↓O₂ + ↑CO₂, respiratory acidosis)
Indications Acute pulmonary oedema / cardiogenic, OSA, CCF AECOPD with respiratory acidosis (pH 7.25–7.35), neuromuscular disease, obesity hypoventilation
The exam rule: CPAP = oxygenation problem (Type 1)  |  BiPAP = ventilation/CO₂ problem (Type 2). COPD exacerbation with acidosis → BiPAP if pH 7.25–7.35; pH <7.25 → consider intubation.
Invasive Mechanical Ventilation
Indications
NIV failed/contraindicated; GCS ≤8 (can't protect airway); refractory hypoxia; haemodynamic instability; cardiac arrest
Access
Endotracheal tube (ETT) for short-term; tracheostomy for prolonged ventilation. Requires sedation ± paralysis.
Key Settings
FiO₂, respiratory rate, tidal volume (~6 mL/kg ideal body weight — lung protective), PEEP, I:E ratio. Aim: shortest duration possible.
ECMO — The Top Rung
Blood removed → oxygenated + CO₂ removed → returned Specialist ECMO centres only Reversible respiratory failure only Bridge to recovery / transplant
Indicated when all other measures have failed and the underlying cause is potentially reversible (e.g. severe ARDS, viral pneumonitis). Not a long-term solution.

CPAP = Type 1 RF (oxygenation — pulmonary oedema, OSA). BiPAP = Type 2 RF (ventilation — COPD + hypercapnia).
BiPAP in COPD: use when pH 7.25–7.35. pH <7.25 → consider intubation. pH >7.35 → medical treatment first.
PEEP = prevents alveolar collapse, recruits lung, improves oxygenation. Added by HFNC, CPAP/BiPAP, and mechanical ventilator.
In COPD exacerbation: drive nebulisers with air not O₂ (avoids worsening hypercapnia)
Escalation ladder: O₂ → HFNC → NIV → mechanical ventilation → ECMO. Never skip steps without clinical indication.
ECMO = reversible failure only, specialist centres. Not a long-term solution — bridge to recovery or transplant.
RESPIRATORY__Respiratory Failure & ARDS:
Respiratory failure = the lungs fail to oxygenate and/or remove CO₂, defined on ABG. The central fork: Type 1 (oxygenation failure) vs Type 2 (ventilation failure) — drives the cause, management, and which NIV to use.
Type 1 vs Type 2 — The Spine
Type 1Type 2
Definition ↓PaO₂ (<8 kPa), normal or low CO₂ ↓PaO₂ + ↑PaCO₂ (>6 kPa)
Problem Oxygenation failure (V/Q mismatch — blood not oxygenated) Ventilation failure (can't blow off CO₂)
Causes Pneumonia, PE, pulmonary oedema, ARDS, asthma (early), ILD COPD (commonest), severe asthma (late/tiring), neuromuscular disease (GBS, MND), opiates, obesity hypoventilation / OSA, chest wall deformity
NIV CPAP (improves oxygenation) BiPAP (actively ventilates — ↓CO₂)
O₂ target 94–98% (standard) 88–92% (controlled — avoid worsening hypercapnia)
The tie-in rule: Type 1 → CPAP (oxygenation problem)  |  Type 2 → BiPAP (ventilation problem). Cross-ref respiratory support notes.
The Danger Sign — Tiring Type 1
Type 1 RF: ↓PaO₂, low/normal CO₂ (patient hyperventilating to compensate)
Patient tires → respiratory muscles fail → can no longer hyperventilate
CO₂ starts to rise → normal or rising CO₂ = danger signal
Progresses to Type 2 RF → exhaustion → arrest
In acute asthma: a normal PCO₂ = life-threatening (patient should be blowing off CO₂; normalisation = exhaustion). Cross-ref asthma management.
Clinical Features
Hypoxia (both types)
Dyspnoea, tachypnoea, cyanosis, confusion/agitation, tachycardia, use of accessory muscles
Hypercapnia (Type 2 specific)
CO₂ retention flap (asterixis — outstretched hands), bounding pulse, warm peripheries (vasodilation), headache, drowsiness → coma ("CO₂ narcosis")
Management Principles
Type 1 — Oxygenation
High-flow O₂ (target 94–98%); CPAP if not responding; treat the cause (e.g. antibiotics for pneumonia, diurese pulmonary oedema); consider HFNC
Type 2 — Ventilation
Controlled O₂ (88–92%); BiPAP for respiratory acidosis (pH 7.25–7.35); treat the cause (bronchodilators for COPD, reverse opiates with naloxone); escalate to intubation if pH <7.25
ARDS = severe Type 1 respiratory failure caused by increased alveolar-capillary permeability → protein-rich fluid floods the alveoli → non-cardiogenic pulmonary oedema → atelectasis, ↓compliance, refractory hypoxia. The heart is fine — the capillaries are leaky.
Aetiology — The Inflammatory Insults
Sepsis / pneumonia (commonest) Aspiration of gastric contents Massive blood transfusion (TRALI) Major trauma / burns Acute pancreatitis COVID-19 Cardiopulmonary bypass
Unifying theme: a massive inflammatory insult (pulmonary or systemic) → diffuse alveolar damage → capillary leak → non-cardiogenic pulmonary oedema
Clinical Features
Acute severe dyspnoea Tachypnoea Refractory hypoxia (doesn't correct with O₂) Bilateral fine crackles Low SpO₂ despite high FiO₂
Refractory hypoxia = hallmark of ARDS — hypoxia that does not correct with supplemental oxygen alone (distinguishes from most other causes of Type 1 RF).
Berlin Criteria — Diagnostic Definition
1. Acute Onset
Within 1 week of a known clinical insult or new/worsening respiratory symptoms
2. Bilateral Infiltrates
CXR or CT — bilateral opacities not fully explained by effusion, lobar collapse, or nodules. Resembles pulmonary oedema + air bronchograms.
3. Non-Cardiogenic
Respiratory failure not fully explained by cardiac failure or fluid overload. Echo or wedge pressure if doubt.
4. PaO₂/FiO₂ Ratio <300 mmHg (<40 kPa)
Mild: 200–300 mmHg · Moderate: 100–200 mmHg · Severe: <100 mmHg. Lower ratio = worse disease.
Management — Supportive (No Specific Cure)
Treat the Cause
Antibiotics for sepsis/pneumonia, amylase monitoring for pancreatitis, stop offending transfusion (TRALI). Cause treatment is the only disease-modifying step.
Lung-Protective Ventilation
Low tidal volume (~6 mL/kg ideal body weight) — avoids volutrauma. Adequate PEEP — prevents repeated alveolar collapse/re-opening. Permissive hypercapnia acceptable.
Prone Positioning
12–16 hours/day — promotes uniform lung inflation, ↓dorsal atelectasis, improves V/Q matching. Mortality benefit in moderate-severe ARDS.
Supportive / ITU
Conservative fluid balance (avoid further oedema); vasopressors; renal support; ECMO if refractory. High mortality (30–60%).

Type 1 = hypoxia alone (oxygenation failure, normal/low CO₂) → CPAP. Type 2 = hypoxia + ↑CO₂ (ventilation failure) → BiPAP.
Tiring Type 1 → rising CO₂ = danger sign (exhaustion). Normal CO₂ in acute asthma = life-threatening.
Type 2 O₂ target: 88–92%. Type 1: 94–98%. Never give high O₂ freely to CO₂ retainers.
CO₂ retention flap (asterixis) = hypercapnia. Bounding pulse + warm peripheries = vasodilation from ↑CO₂.

Berlin criteria: acute (<1 wk) + bilateral infiltrates + non-cardiogenic + PaO₂/FiO₂ <300 mmHg
ARDS causes: sepsis/pneumonia (commonest), pancreatitis, aspiration, TRALI, trauma
ARDS Rx: low tidal volume (6 mL/kg) + PEEP + prone positioning; treat cause; ITU. No specific cure.
Refractory hypoxia = ARDS hallmark. Doesn't correct with supplemental O₂ alone.
Prone positioning: 12–16h/day — mortality benefit in moderate-severe ARDS (improved V/Q, ↓dorsal atelectasis)
RESPIRATORY__Upper Respiratory Tract Epi:
Overview — Respiratory Epithelium

The upper (conducting) airway is lined mostly by respiratory epithelium — pseudostratified ciliated columnar epithelium with goblet cells (often abbreviated PCCE). Its job is to condition inspired air (warm, humidify, filter) and to run the mucociliary escalator that clears trapped debris.

🔬 Image slot — respiratory epithelium — pseudostratified ciliated columnar with goblet cells on a thick basement membrane
Where it is found
  • Respiratory epithelium (PCCE): most of the nasal cavity, paranasal sinuses, nasopharynx, larynx (below the vocal cords), trachea and bronchi.
  • Stratified squamous where there is abrasion/airflow stress: nasal vestibule (keratinised), oropharynx, and the true vocal cords.
  • Olfactory epithelium (specialised) in the roof of the nasal cavity.
“Respiratory epithelium” and “pseudostratified ciliated columnar epithelium with goblet cells” are the same thing — the exam-classic lining of the conducting airways.
How to Recognise It on a Slide ⭐
🔬 Image slot — high-power respiratory epithelium showing cilia, goblet cells and nuclei at different levels
  • Pseudostratified — every cell touches the basement membrane, but the nuclei sit at different levels, giving a false impression of layering.
  • Cilia form a fuzzy pink border on the apical surface (taller than microvilli).
  • Goblet cells — pale/clear, cup-shaped, mucin at the top and the nucleus squashed to the base.
  • A characteristically thick (hyaline) basement membrane below the epithelium.
  • Underlying lamina propria is vascular with seromucous glands.
Pseudostratified vs truly stratified: if you can trace every cell down to the basement membrane it is pseudostratified; in true stratified epithelium the surface cells do not reach it.
The Cell Types of Respiratory Epithelium
CellFeature & role
Ciliated columnarMost numerous; ~200–300 cilia each; drive the mucociliary escalator toward the pharynx
Goblet cellUnicellular gland; secretes mucins (the gel layer of mucus); PAS/Alcian-blue positive
Basal cellStem/reserve cell sitting on the basement membrane; regenerates the other cell types (does not reach the surface)
Brush cellColumnar cell with blunt microvilli; a sensory receptor with a nerve ending at its base (chemosensory)
Small granule (neuroendocrine / Kulchitsky) cellPart of the DNES; contains dense-core granules (serotonin, bombesin); origin of carcinoid / small-cell carcinoma
The basal cell is why the epithelium looks pseudostratified — short cells wedged at the base keep some nuclei low while columnar-cell nuclei sit higher.
The Mucociliary Escalator
🔬 Image slot — mucociliary escalator — gel + sol (periciliary) layers and the direction of ciliary beat
The mucus blanket
  • Sol (periciliary) layer — watery; cilia beat within it
  • Gel layer on top — sticky mucus (goblet cells + glands) that traps particles & microbes
Ciliary beat
  • Fast forward power stroke tips the gel layer toward the pharynx; slow recovery stroke within the sol
  • Mucus is swallowed or expectorated
Cilium ultrastructure
  • “9 + 2” axoneme — nine peripheral microtubule doublets + a central pair.
  • Dynein arms use ATP to slide doublets → bending; anchored by a basal body.
  • Defective dynein → immotile cilia (see clinical box).
Regional Epithelia of the Upper Tract
🔬 Image slot — sagittal nasal cavity showing vestibule / respiratory / olfactory regions
RegionEpithelium
Nasal vestibuleStratified squamous keratinised + hairs (vibrissae) & sebaceous glands
Respiratory region (most of nasal cavity, sinuses, nasopharynx, trachea, bronchi)Pseudostratified ciliated columnar with goblet cells
Olfactory region (roof)Specialised olfactory epithelium (tall pseudostratified: receptor neurons, sustentacular, basal cells; Bowman’s glands)
Oropharynx & true vocal cordsStratified squamous non-keratinised (abrasion resistance)
EpiglottisSquamous on the lingual/upper surface → respiratory on the lower
The true vocal cords are covered by stratified squamous epithelium to withstand vibration — a favourite exam contrast with the respiratory epithelium above and below them.
Lamina Propria & Air-Conditioning
  • Seromucous glands in the lamina propria/submucosa add watery & mucous secretion — humidification.
  • Rich venous plexuses / swell bodies in the nasal conchae warm the air and cause the alternating nasal cycle (and blockage in rhinitis).
  • Vibrissae and the mucus blanket filter particles.
  • Waldeyer’s ring (pharyngeal/palatine/tubal/lingual tonsils) — MALT guarding the entrance to the aerodigestive tract.
Three functions to remember for the nose: warm, humidify, filter — delivered by vasculature, glands and the mucociliary blanket respectively.
Stains
  • H&E — cilia, goblet cells and the thick basement membrane.
  • PAS / Alcian blue — goblet-cell & gland mucins (magenta / blue); highlights goblet-cell density.
  • Immunohistochemistry — chromogranin / synaptophysin for neuroendocrine (small granule) cells; cytokeratins for epithelial tumours.
Clinical / Pathological Correlate
Squamous metaplasia
Smoking replaces ciliated/goblet epithelium with stratified squamous → loss of clearance; a step toward dysplasia & SCC
Primary ciliary dyskinesia
Dynein-arm defect → immotile cilia. Kartagener: situs inversus + bronchiectasis + sinusitis + infertility
Allergic rhinitis
Type I hypersensitivity → oedema, eosinophils, goblet-cell & gland hypersecretion
Nasal polyps
Oedematous inflamed respiratory mucosa; associated with chronic rhinosinusitis, aspirin sensitivity, CF
Sinusitis
Impaired drainage/ciliary clearance → infection of sinus respiratory mucosa
Epistaxis (Little’s area)
Kiesselbach’s plexus on the anterior septum — commonest nosebleed site
Metaplasia is adaptive but costly: squamous cells resist smoke but cannot clear mucus, so smokers accumulate secretions and infections — and squamous change can progress to carcinoma.
⭐ Exam Pearls
Respiratory epithelium = pseudostratified ciliated columnar with goblet cells. Every cell touches the basement membrane.
Five cell types: ciliated (most), goblet, basal (stem), brush (sensory microvilli), small-granule/neuroendocrine.
Basal cells are the stem cells and the reason it looks “stratified”.
Cilia have a 9 + 2 axoneme moved by dynein; the escalator sweeps mucus to the pharynx.
True vocal cords & oropharynx = stratified squamous (abrasion); nasal vestibule = keratinised squamous.
Nose functions: warm (venous plexus), humidify (glands), filter (vibrissae + mucus).
Smoking → squamous metaplasia → lost clearance → dysplasia/SCC.
Kartagener (dynein defect): situs inversus + bronchiectasis + sinusitis + infertility.
RESPIRATORY__Bronchi & Bronchioles:
Overview — The Conducting Tree

Below the trachea the airway branches repeatedly, and its wall changes in a predictable, graded way at each level. Knowing the trend lets you place any airway on a slide.

🔬 Image slot — airway tree — trachea → bronchi → bronchioles → terminal → respiratory bronchiole

2

3

The four trends going distal: epithelium gets shorter (columnar → cuboidal), cartilage & glands disappear, goblet cells disappear, and smooth muscle becomes relatively more prominent.
How to Place an Airway on a Slide ⭐
🔬 Image slot — side-by-side bronchus (cartilage + glands) vs bronchiole (no cartilage, thick smooth muscle)
It is a BRONCHUS if…
  • Cartilage plates in the wall
  • Submucosal seromucous glands
  • Pseudostratified ciliated columnar epithelium with goblet cells
  • A discrete band of smooth muscle between mucosa & cartilage
It is a BRONCHIOLE if…
  • No cartilage, no glands
  • Smooth muscle looks relatively thick for the wall
  • Epithelium simple ciliated columnar → cuboidal; club cells; few/no goblet cells
  • Often a folded (scalloped) lumen from muscle contraction
The single best discriminator: cartilage & glands = bronchus; their absence = bronchiole.

🔬 Image slot — bronchiole — simple columnar/cuboidal epithelium over a prominent smooth-muscle layer, no cartilage
  • ≤1 mm diameter; no cartilage, no glands, no goblet cells in the terminal bronchiole.
  • Epithelium: simple ciliated columnar proximally → simple cuboidal (often ciliated) distally.
  • Relatively thick smooth-muscle layer (Reisseissen’s muscle) — controls airway calibre and, because there is no cartilage to splint them open, bronchioles are the airways that collapse/constrict in asthma.
  • Held open by radial traction (elastic recoil of the surrounding alveoli), not by cartilage.
  • Terminal bronchiole = the last conducting airway; each supplies a pulmonary lobule.
Because their patency depends on smooth-muscle tone and elastic traction rather than cartilage, small airways are the critical site of obstruction in asthma and COPD.
Club (Clara) Cells
🔬 Image slot — club (Clara) cell — dome-shaped non-ciliated cell bulging into the bronchiolar lumen
  • Dome-shaped, non-ciliated cells that bulge into the lumen; increase in number distally.
  • Secrete a surfactant-like material & club-cell secretory protein (CC16) → reduce surface tension & protect the small-airway lining.
  • Detoxify inhaled xenobiotics via cytochrome P450.
  • Act as progenitor (stem) cells that regenerate bronchiolar epithelium.
Think of the club cell as the bronchiolar all-rounder: secretion + detoxification + stem cell — the small-airway counterpart of the goblet cell (which it replaces).

  • Everything from the respiratory bronchiole distal to one terminal bronchiole = the pulmonary acinus, the functional gas-exchange unit.

Asthma
Bronchiolar smooth-muscle hypertrophy + bronchoconstriction, mucus plugging, eosinophils; Curschmann spirals & Charcot-Leyden crystals in sputum
Chronic bronchitis

Bronchiectasis

Bronchiolitis / small-airways disease

COPD

⭐ Exam Pearls
Cartilage + glands = bronchus; neither = bronchiole. The one distinction that answers most questions.
Going distal: epithelium shortens, cartilage/glands/goblet cells disappear, smooth muscle becomes relatively prominent.
Terminal bronchiole = last conducting airway; respiratory bronchiole = first gas exchange (alveoli in the wall).
Club (Clara) cells replace goblet cells distally: secretion + P450 detox + stem cell.
Bronchioles have no cartilage → held open by elastic radial traction; they collapse/constrict in asthma & COPD.
The acinus (respiratory bronchiole & distal) is the gas-exchange unit; the lobule is supplied by one terminal bronchiole.
Chronic bronchitis = ↑ Reid index (gland hypertrophy); asthma = smooth-muscle hypertrophy + mucus + eosinophils.

RESPIRATORY__Alveoli & Blood-Air Barrier:
Overview — The Gas-Exchange Surface

Alveoli are the thin-walled air sacs where gas is exchanged. There are ~300 million of them, giving a total surface area of ~70 m² — the whole design is built to make diffusion large in area and short in distance.

🔬 Image slot — lung parenchyma at low power — thin-walled alveoli opening off alveolar ducts & sacs
  • Alveoli open off respiratory bronchioles → alveolar ducts → alveolar sacs.
  • Adjacent alveoli share an interalveolar septum containing the capillary network.
  • Gas exchange obeys Fick’s law: rate ∝ (area × Δpressure) ÷ thickness — so the barrier is kept huge and thin.
Everything about the alveolus is optimised for diffusion: a massive surface area, an ultra-thin (~0.2 µm) blood–air barrier, and a dense capillary bed.
How to Recognise It on a Slide ⭐
🔬 Image slot — interalveolar septum — flat type I pneumocytes, plump type II cells, septal capillary with RBCs
  • Empty, thin-walled air spaces separated by delicate septa.
  • Septa contain capillaries packed with red cells — the pink profiles in the wall.
  • Type I pneumocytes — you mostly see their flat nuclei bulging into the space (cytoplasm too thin to resolve).
  • Type II pneumocytes — rounded, cuboidal cells at septal corners, with foamy/vacuolated cytoplasm.
  • Alveolar macrophages — large cells free in the airspace, often with brown/black particulate.
On routine H&E you usually identify type I cells only by their nuclei; the gas-exchange cytoplasm is below the resolution of the light microscope.

Type II pneumocyteCuboidal; surfactant (lamellar bodies); stem cell for both types; ~5% of area but more numerous

The septum has a thin side (fused basement membranes → efficient gas exchange) and a thick side (interstitium with fluid/elastic → structural support & fluid handling).
The Blood–Air Barrier
🔬 Image slot — blood-air barrier ultrastructure (EM) — type I pneumocyte, fused basal lamina, capillary endothelium

To reach haemoglobin, oxygen crosses just three thin layers (total ~0.2–0.5 µm):

Anything that thickens this barrier (oedema fluid, fibrosis, hyaline membrane) or reduces its area (emphysema) impairs diffusion — the structural basis of hypoxaemia.
Type I vs Type II Pneumocytes
Type I (membranous)
  • Simple squamous, extremely thin
  • ~95% of surface area, ~40% of cell number
  • The gas-exchange cell; joined by tight junctions
  • Cannot divide — if killed, replaced by type II
Type II (granular)
  • Cuboidal, at septal corners; lamellar bodies
  • ~5% of area, ~60% of cell number
  • Make & secrete surfactant
  • Stem cell — regenerate type I and type II
Full detail is in the dedicated Type I & II Pneumocytes note — here, remember: I = thin gas exchange, II = surfactant + repair.
Surfactant — Keeping Alveoli Open
  • A phospholipid–protein film (chiefly dipalmitoylphosphatidylcholine, DPPC, + surfactant proteins A–D) made by type II cells and stored in lamellar bodies.
  • Lowers surface tension at the air–liquid interface → prevents alveolar collapse (atelectasis) at end-expiration and reduces the work of breathing.
  • Laplace’s law (P = 2T/r): small alveoli would empty into large ones; surfactant lowers T more in small alveoli → keeps them stable.
  • Appears ~24 weeks, adequate by ~35 weeks — timing that governs neonatal risk.
Surfactant proteins A & D are also innate-immune opsonins (collectins); B & C spread the lipid film.
Alveolar Macrophages & Pores of Kohn
🔬 Image slot — alveolar macrophage (dust cell) free in the airspace; pore of Kohn between adjacent alveoli
Alveolar macrophage (dust cell)
  • Monocyte-derived; phagocytoses dust, microbes & spent surfactant
  • Migrate up the mucociliary escalator or into lymphatics
  • In pulmonary congestion become heart-failure cells (haemosiderin-laden)
Pores of Kohn
  • Small holes connecting adjacent alveoli → collateral air flow
  • Also let macrophages, fluid & infection spread between alveoli
Stains
  • H&E — thin septa, capillaries, pneumocyte nuclei, macrophages; hyaline membranes as glassy pink lining in DAD.
  • Elastic stains (EVG) — the septal elastic network (lost in emphysema).
  • Perls’ Prussian blue — haemosiderin in heart-failure cells (blue).
  • TTF-1 (IHC) — marks type II pneumocytes & lung adenocarcinoma.
Clinical / Pathological Correlate
Neonatal RDS
Surfactant deficiency (prematurity) → atelectasis + hyaline membranes; treat with antenatal steroids & surfactant
ARDS (diffuse alveolar damage)
Type I pneumocyte death, protein-rich exudate, hyaline membranes → refractory hypoxaemia
Emphysema
Septal destruction → loss of surface area & elastic recoil → impaired exchange
Pulmonary oedema
Fluid in the interstitium/airspaces thickens the barrier → impaired diffusion
Pulmonary fibrosis
Septal collagen deposition widens the barrier → restrictive defect, low DLCO
Heart-failure cells
Haemosiderin-laden alveolar macrophages in chronic pulmonary venous congestion
Hyaline membranes (glassy eosinophilic alveolar lining of dead cells + plasma protein) are the shared histological signature of ARDS and neonatal RDS.
⭐ Exam Pearls
The blood–air barrier = type I pneumocyte → fused basement membrane → capillary endothelium (~0.2–0.5 µm).
Type I = 95% of surface, gas exchange, can’t divide; Type II = surfactant + stem cell (regenerate type I).
Surfactant (DPPC, from type II lamellar bodies) lowers surface tension → prevents atelectasis; adequate by ~35 weeks.
By Laplace, surfactant stabilises small alveoli so they don’t empty into large ones.
Hyaline membranes = ARDS & neonatal RDS; both involve barrier injury.
Dust cells = alveolar macrophages; haemosiderin-laden ones = heart-failure cells (Perls’ positive).
Pores of Kohn allow collateral airflow — and spread of infection/exudate.
Barrier disease: thicken it (oedema/fibrosis) or lose area (emphysema) → hypoxaemia.
RESPIRATORY__Type I & II Pneumocytes:
Overview — Two Cells, One Lining

The alveolar surface is lined by a continuous epithelial sheet of just two cells, sealed by tight junctions that keep the alveolus dry:

🔬 Image slot — type I (flat, squamous) vs type II (cuboidal, granular) pneumocytes side by side in an alveolar wall
Type I — the surface
  • Thin squamous cell for gas exchange
  • Covers most of the area; terminally differentiated
Type II — the caretaker
  • Surfactant, fluid clearance, defence
  • The alveolar stem cell — repairs the lining
One-line division of labour: Type I = thin gas-exchange surface; Type II = surfactant + stem cell + housekeeping.
How to Recognise Each ⭐
🔬 Image slot — high-power alveolar wall labelling a flat type I nucleus vs a cuboidal foamy type II cell at the corner
Type I
  • Only the flattened nucleus is visible, bulging into the airspace
  • Cytoplasm too thin (~0.1–0.2 µm) to resolve on light microscopy
  • Lines the long, smooth stretches of septum
Type II
  • Rounded / cuboidal, sits in septal corners/niches
  • Foamy, vacuolated cytoplasm (dissolved lamellar-body lipid)
  • Apical surface bulges (“dome”); may look like a fried egg
On EM the diagnosis is easy: type II cells contain lamellar bodies (whorled, osmiophilic) and apical microvilli; type I cells are a thin rim with pinocytotic vesicles.
Type I Pneumocyte (Membranous)
  • Simple squamous; ~95% of alveolar surface but only ~40% of cell number.
  • Extremely attenuated cytoplasm forms the thin side of the blood–air barrier; rich in pinocytotic vesicles & caveolae (fluid/solute handling).
  • Joined to neighbours by occluding tight junctions → a barrier that keeps fluid out of the airspace.
  • Terminally differentiated — cannot divide. When killed it is replaced by a proliferating type II cell that then transdifferentiates.
  • Markers: AQP5 (aquaporin-5), podoplanin (T1α), caveolin-1.
Because it cannot divide and is so thin, the type I cell is the vulnerable cell of the alveolus — the first to die in diffuse alveolar damage.
Type II Pneumocyte (Granular)
🔬 Image slot — type II pneumocyte ultrastructure — apical microvilli, RER/Golgi, lamellar bodies
  • Cuboidal with short apical microvilli; ~5% of area but ~60% of cell number (the more numerous cell).
  • Abundant RER & Golgi and the diagnostic lamellar bodies (membrane-bound, osmiophilic whorls that store surfactant).
Four jobs
Surfactant — synthesise, secrete & recycle it
Stem cell — self-renew & differentiate into type I (repair)
Fluid clearance — ENaC + Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase pump fluid out of the alveolus (keeps it dry)
Defence — secrete SP-A/SP-D; metabolise xenobiotics
Markers: surfactant proteins (SP-B, SP-C), TTF-1 and Napsin A — the same markers used to identify lung adenocarcinoma.

🔬 Image slot — type II hyperplasia lining a damaged alveolus (reparative response)
  • Because type I cells cannot divide, repair depends on type II proliferation → transdifferentiation into type I.
  • Acute injury therefore shows type II (pneumocyte) hyperplasia — a plump cuboidal lining replacing the flat one.
  • Aberrant / repeated repair drives fibrosis (fibroblast recruitment) rather than clean re-epithelialisation.
Reactive type II hyperplasia can mimic malignancy on cytology — a known diagnostic pitfall after ARDS or infection.

Neonatal RDS
Immature type II cells → surfactant deficiency → atelectasis + hyaline membranes; SP-B gene deficiency is fatal
ARDS / diffuse alveolar damage

Repeated alveolar injury with type II hyperplasia & aberrant repair → honeycomb fibrosis

Surfactant is ~90% lipid (DPPC) + SP-A–D; SP-B forms tubular myelin and its deficiency is lethal in neonates.

TTF-1 & Napsin A mark type II cells and lung adenocarcinoma.

RESPIRATORY__Goblet Cells & Cilia:
Overview — The Two Partners of Mucociliary Clearance

Airway defence rests on a partnership: goblet cells make the sticky mucus that traps particles, and cilia move it toward the pharynx. Together they form the mucociliary escalator — the airway’s primary innate defence.

🔬 Image slot — respiratory epithelium showing ciliated cells and interspersed goblet cells (the escalator team)
Goblet cell = the flypaper
  • Unicellular gland secreting gel-forming mucins
  • Traps inhaled particles, microbes & irritants
Cilia = the conveyor
  • Motile apical projections
  • Beat in coordinated waves to sweep mucus out
Break either partner and clearance fails: bad cilia (primary ciliary dyskinesia) or bad mucus (cystic fibrosis) both cause recurrent infection & bronchiectasis.
How to Recognise Them ⭐
🔬 Image slot — high-power view — pale cup-shaped goblet cells beside the eosinophilic ciliary fringe
Goblet cell
  • Pale / clear, cup-shaped (“goblet”) profile
  • Apical theca distended with mucin; nucleus squashed to the base
  • PAS-magenta / Alcian-blue positive
Cilia
  • Fuzzy eosinophilic fringe on the apical surface
  • A dark line of basal bodies just beneath (the terminal-web level)
  • Taller than microvilli; motile
Both sit at the apical pole, but the goblet cell is a secretory cell (no cilia) while the ciliated cell carries the motile fringe — they alternate along the epithelium.
Goblet Cell — Structure & Secretion
🔬 Image slot — goblet cell ultrastructure — basal RER/Golgi/nucleus and an apical theca of mucinogen granules
  • A unicellular exocrine gland: narrow base with the nucleus + abundant RER & Golgi, widening into an apical theca packed with mucinogen granules.
  • Secretes gel-forming mucins (chiefly MUC5AC; submucosal glands add MUC5B) by merocrine exocytosis.
  • Mucins are huge glycoproteins that swell 100–1000× on hydration to form the sticky gel layer.
  • Secretion is up-regulated by irritants & inflammation (smoke, infection) → more mucus.
  • Goblet cells are numerous in the trachea/bronchi and disappear by the bronchioles (club cells take over).
The mucus blanket also carries antimicrobials — lysozyme, lactoferrin, defensins and secretory IgA — so it is chemical as well as physical defence.
The Cilium — Axoneme Architecture
🔬 Image slot — cilium cross-section (EM) — 9+2 axoneme with outer & inner dynein arms, radial spokes, nexin
  • “9 + 2” axoneme: nine peripheral microtubule doublets (an A tubule + an incomplete B tubule) around a central pair.
  • Dynein arms (outer & inner, ODA/IDA) project from the A tubule — the ATPase motors that drive beating.
  • Radial spokes link doublets to the central sheath; nexin (dynein-regulatory) links tie adjacent doublets together.
  • Anchored by a basal body (nine microtubule triplets, derived from a centriole) with a ciliary rootlet.
  • ~200–300 cilia per cell, each ~5–10 µm long.
Compare the basal body (9 triplets, 9×3, no central pair) with the axoneme (9 doublets + 2, 9×2 + 2) — a classic exam contrast.
How Cilia Beat & Move Mucus
🔬 Image slot — metachronal wave — rows of cilia beating in sequence to sweep the gel layer toward the pharynx
  • Dynein arms walk along the adjacent B tubule using ATP; because nexin restrains sliding, the doublets bend instead.
  • Biphasic beat: a fast, stiff power stroke (tip engages the gel layer) then a slow, curled recovery stroke within the watery sol.
  • Neighbouring cilia beat slightly out of phase → a metachronal wave that propels mucus at ~1 cm/min toward the pharynx (frequency ~12–15 Hz).
  • Beating needs a normal periciliary (sol) depth — dehydrated mucus (CF) collapses the cilia and clearance stalls even when the cilia are structurally normal.
Two layers must be right: cilia beat within the watery sol and their tips grip the overlying sticky gel. Get the hydration wrong and the escalator jams.

Only cilia are motile and microtubule-based; microvilli & stereocilia are non-motile actin projections (“stereocilia” are misnamed — they are giant microvilli, not cilia).
Clinical / Pathological Correlate
Primary ciliary dyskinesia
Dynein-arm (ODA/IDA) defect → immotile cilia; nasal brushing/EM diagnostic
Kartagener syndrome
PCD subset: situs inversus + bronchiectasis + chronic sinusitis (± infertility, otitis media)
Cystic fibrosis
CFTR defect → dehydrated, thick mucus; cilia are normal but the escalator jams → bronchiectasis
Goblet-cell hyperplasia / metaplasia
Chronic irritation (smoking, asthma, chronic bronchitis) → more/ectopic goblet cells & mucus hypersecretion
Smoking & ciliary loss
Smoke paralyses & strips cilia and triggers squamous metaplasia → impaired clearance, morning cough
Male infertility
The sperm flagellum shares the 9+2 axoneme, so PCD often causes immotile sperm
PCD vs CF — the key contrast: both give bronchiectasis & sinusitis, but PCD is a ciliary (motor) defect while CF is a mucus (hydration) defect with structurally normal cilia.

Goblet cells are plentiful in trachea/bronchi and absent by the bronchioles (club cells replace them).
Cilium = 9 + 2 axoneme; dynein arms are the ATPase motors; nexin converts sliding into bending.
Basal body = 9 triplets (like a centriole); axoneme = 9 doublets + 2.
Cilia beat with a power + recovery stroke as a metachronal wave (~1 cm/min toward the pharynx).
PCD (Kartagener) = dynein defect → immotile cilia + situs inversus, bronchiectasis, sinusitis, infertility.
CF = normal cilia but dehydrated mucus (CFTR) → escalator jams; contrast with PCD.

RESPIRATORY__Lung Parenchyma:
Overview — Putting the Lung Together

Parenchyma = the functional gas-exchange tissue (respiratory bronchioles, alveolar ducts, sacs & alveoli), held in an elastic connective-tissue framework and served by a dual blood supply. This note assembles the individual cells & airways of the earlier notes into the organ.

🔬 Image slot — low-power lung — vast pale airspaces, delicate septa, a bronchovascular bundle and the pleural edge
  • Conducting portion (no exchange): trachea → bronchi → bronchioles → terminal bronchioles.
  • Respiratory portion / parenchyma (exchange): respiratory bronchioles → alveolar ducts → alveolar sacs → alveoli.
  • Everything is embedded in an elastic stroma and wrapped by the pleura.
Two design themes to carry through: the lung is built for elastic recoil (to drive expiration) and for maximal thin-walled surface area (to drive diffusion).
How to Read Lung Architecture ⭐
🔬 Image slot — bronchovascular bundle — a bronchiole travelling with its accompanying pulmonary artery branch
  • Vast pale airspaces with delicate, capillary-rich septa = alveolar parenchyma.
  • A bronchovascular bundle: an airway always travels with a branch of the pulmonary artery of similar calibre — find one, the other is beside it.
  • Pulmonary veins run alone, out in the interlobular septa (not with the airway).
  • The pleura is the thin mesothelium-covered edge of the section.
  • Scattered black specks = anthracotic (carbon-laden) macrophages.
Artery-with-airway, vein-apart: the pulmonary artery accompanies the bronchus/bronchiole; the pulmonary vein sits at the periphery of the lobule — a reliable orientation clue.
The Organisational Units
UnitDefinitionWhy it matters
AcinusEverything distal to one terminal bronchiole (respiratory bronchioles → alveoli)The functional gas-exchange unit
Pulmonary lobuleRegion supplied by one terminal bronchiole, bounded by interlobular septaUnit of HRCT interpretation; septa carry veins & lymphatics
Bronchopulmonary segmentRegion supplied by a segmental bronchus + its own arterySurgically resectable unit (segmentectomy)
🔬 Image slot — diagram of a pulmonary lobule / bronchopulmonary segment with interlobular septa
Distribution of disease follows these units: centriacinar vs panacinar emphysema; lobar vs lobular (broncho) pneumonia.
The Pleura
🔬 Image slot — pleura — a single layer of flat mesothelial cells over subserosal elastic connective tissue
  • A serous membrane of simple squamous mesothelium over a thin elastic connective-tissue layer.
  • Visceral pleura covers the lung; parietal pleura lines the chest wall; the potential pleural cavity between them holds a film of serous fluid (lubrication).
Visceral pleura
  • Blood: bronchial (+pulmonary); nerves: autonomic → insensate to pain
Parietal pleura
  • Blood: systemic; nerves: somatic (intercostal, phrenic) → pain-sensitive
Pleuritic chest pain comes from the parietal pleura (somatic innervation); the visceral pleura is insensitive — and mesothelium is the cell of origin of mesothelioma (asbestos).
A Dual Blood Supply
🔬 Image slot — dual circulation schematic — pulmonary (gas exchange) vs bronchial (nutritive) vessels
Pulmonary circulation
  • Deoxygenated blood for gas exchange
  • Low pressure, high flow (whole cardiac output)
  • Arteries run with the airways (bronchovascular bundle); veins return in interlobular septa
Bronchial circulation
  • Systemic, oxygenated blood that nourishes airways, vessels & pleura
  • Small, high-pressure branches of the aorta
The lung is unusual: the vessels doing the work (pulmonary) carry deoxygenated blood, while a separate bronchial supply keeps the tissue alive — which is why pulmonary emboli rarely infarct the (dually-supplied) lung unless the bronchial supply is also compromised.
Elastic Framework, Interstitium & Lymphatics
  • A continuous elastic-fibre network runs from the pleura through the septa around airways & vessels → provides recoil and holds bronchioles open by radial traction.
  • Interstitium = the connective tissue of the septa: a thin (exchange) side and a thick side with collagen, elastin, fibroblasts, macrophages, mast cells and occasional lymphocytes.
  • Lymphatics form two plexuses — a superficial (pleural) and a deep (bronchovascular) network — draining to hilar nodes; there are no lymphatics in the alveolar wall itself.
  • BALT (bronchus-associated lymphoid tissue) guards the airways.
Two failure modes of the framework: lose elastin → emphysema (floppy, over-inflated); expand the interstitium with collagen → fibrosis (stiff, restricted).
Stains
  • H&E — overall architecture; airspaces, septa, bronchovascular bundles, pleura.
  • Elastic stains (Verhoeff–van Gieson / orcein) — the elastic framework & pleural elastica; shows destruction in emphysema and helps stage pleural invasion by tumour.
  • Masson trichrome — interstitial collagen / fibrosis (blue) — used in ILD.
  • Calretinin / WT-1 (IHC) — mesothelial markers (mesothelioma vs adenocarcinoma).
Clinical / Pathological Correlate
Emphysema
Elastin destruction & alveolar-wall loss → permanent airspace enlargement, ↓ recoil (centriacinar = smoking; panacinar = α1-antitrypsin)
Interstitial lung disease / IPF
Interstitial collagen deposition → stiff lungs, honeycombing (UIP pattern); restrictive defect, low DLCO
Pneumonia
Alveolar exudate (consolidation): lobar (whole lobe) vs bronchopneumonia (patchy, lobular)
Pneumothorax
Air in the pleural cavity → lung collapses (loss of the negative intrapleural pressure)
Mesothelioma
Malignancy of pleural mesothelium (asbestos); calretinin/WT-1 positive
Anthracosis
Harmless carbon accumulation in macrophages & septa; heavy dust exposure → pneumoconiosis
Obstructive vs restrictive at the tissue level: emphysema destroys the elastic parenchyma (obstructive, air-trapping); fibrosis stiffens the interstitium (restrictive) — opposite architectural failures.
⭐ Exam Pearls
Parenchyma = gas-exchange tissue (respiratory bronchiole → alveoli); the rest is conducting/stroma.
Bronchovascular bundle: airway travels with the pulmonary artery; the pulmonary vein runs alone in interlobular septa.
Acinus = distal to one terminal bronchiole (gas exchange); lobule = supplied by one terminal bronchiole; bronchopulmonary segment = resectable unit.
Pleura = simple squamous mesothelium; parietal pleura is pain-sensitive (somatic), visceral is insensate.
Dual supply: pulmonary (deoxygenated, exchange) + bronchial (systemic, nutritive) — why PE rarely infarcts the lung.
Elastic framework gives recoil; lose elastin → emphysema, expand interstitium with collagen → fibrosis.
No lymphatics in the alveolar wall; two plexuses (pleural + bronchovascular) drain to hilar nodes.
Mesothelioma (asbestos) is calretinin/WT-1 positive; anthracosis = harmless carbon.
